$$
and
$$
\boxed{J=2.8125\,\mathrm J}.
$$
The origin is a strict effective-potential minimum exactly when
$k-m\Omega^2>0$. At equality it is marginal in the radial quadratic model; above it the origin is unstable. As $\Omega\to0$, $U_{\rm eff}\to U$ and $J$ becomes ordinary inertial mechanical energy.
rubricCriteria: Derives the rotating equation and identifies the centrifugal term as part of the effective potential.
Proves conservation by a velocity dot product that explicitly annihilates Coriolis power.
Computes both energy contributions, the Jacobi value, and the origin's exact stability condition.

commonErrors.description: Adds rather than subtracts the centrifugal potential from $U$.
commonErrors.consequence: The effective force points inward and the rotating-frame stability threshold is reversed.

commonErrors.description: Includes the Coriolis force in a scalar potential energy.
commonErrors.consequence: A velocity-dependent perpendicular force is misrepresented and the conservation proof becomes invalid.

problems.flawedProof: The effective potential is $U+m\Omega^2r^2/2$ because centrifugal acceleration points outward. Coriolis force has potential $2m\Omega xy$, so ordinary rotating-frame kinetic plus $U$ is conserved.

problems.title: Foucault precession retains only Earth's vertical rotation component
problems.objective: Local rotating-frame linearization derives the Foucault equations, precession direction, latitude law, and the approximation that discards vertical motion.
problems.statement:
Use local axes $x$ east, $y$ north, and $z$ upward at latitude $\lambda$. Earth's angular velocity has local components
$$
\boldsymbol\Omega=(0,\Omega\cos\lambda,\Omega\sin\lambda).
$$
A long pendulum of length $\ell$ executes small horizontal oscillations, with vertical displacement second order in amplitude. Starting from the rotating-frame equation, derive the coupled leading-order equations for $x$ and $y$. State which terms are neglected and why.

Use a complex coordinate to show that the oscillation plane precesses relative to Earth at angular rate $-\Omega\sin\lambda$ with the sign convention that positive angles turn east toward north. Give the precession period and its equatorial and polar limits.

For $\ell=10.0\,\mathrm m$, $g=9.81\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$, $\lambda=45.0^\circ$, and $\Omega=7.2921159\times10^{-5}\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$, compute the fast pendulum frequency and Foucault precession period in hours.
permittedResults: For small pendulum angles, the horizontal restoring acceleration is $-(g/ell)(x,y)$.
problems.strategy: Project Coriolis acceleration onto the local horizontal plane, retain only terms first order in oscillation amplitude and Earth's rotation rate, then remove the slow phase with a complex exponential.
hints: For horizontal velocity, $(-2\boldsymbol\Omega\times\mathbf v)_h=(2\Omega\sin\lambda\,\dot y,-2\Omega\sin\lambda\,\dot x)$.
With $z_c=x+iy$ and $f=\Omega\sin\lambda$, the equation is $\ddot z_c+2if\dot z_c+\omega_0^2z_c=0$.
The horizontal component of Earth's rotation couples to vertical velocity, which is beyond the retained small-angle order here.
problems.solution:
To leading order, the pendulum restoring acceleration is
$-(g/\ell)(x,y)$. With horizontal velocity $(\dot x,\dot y,0)$,
$$
-2\boldsymbol\Omega\times\mathbf v
=(2\Omega\sin\lambda\,\dot y,
-2\Omega\sin\lambda\,\dot x,
2\Omega\cos\lambda\,\dot x).
$$
The vertical component is absorbed by tension and the second-order vertical kinematics. Centrifugal changes are already included in measured local $g$, and terms of order $\Omega^2$ are neglected. Thus
$$
\boxed{\ddot x+\omega_0^2x=2f\dot y},
\qquad
\boxed{\ddot y+\omega_0^2y=-2f\dot x},
$$
where $\omega_0=\sqrt{g/\ell}$ and $f=\Omega\sin\lambda$.

For $z_c=x+iy$,
$$
\ddot z_c+2if\dot z_c+\omega_0^2z_c=0.
$$
Writing $z_c=e^{-ift}w$ leaves
$\ddot w+(\omega_0^2+f^2)w=0$. Hence the fast oscillation is viewed through a slowly rotating factor $e^{-ift}$, so the plane precesses at
$$
\boxed{\Omega_F=-\Omega\sin\lambda}.
$$
It is clockwise in the northern hemisphere with the stated orientation convention. The period is
$$
\boxed{T_F=\frac{2\pi}{\Omega|\sin\lambda|}}.
$$
It diverges at the equator and equals one sidereal day at a pole.

Numerically,
$$
\omega_0=\sqrt{9.81/10.0}=\boxed{0.9905\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}},
$$
and
$$
T_F=\frac{2\pi}{(7.2921159\times10^{-5})\sin45^\circ}
=1.218\times10^5\,\mathrm s
=\boxed{33.85\,\mathrm h}.
$$
The scale separation $\Omega/\omega_0\ll1$ validates the slow-precession approximation.
rubricCriteria: Projects Earth's rotation vector and obtains both horizontal Coriolis signs in the small-angle equations.
Uses the complex equation to extract the slow precession factor, direction, and latitude dependence.
Computes the oscillation and precession scales and states the neglected orders and limiting latitudes.

commonErrors.description: Uses the full Earth rotation rate instead of its local vertical component.
commonErrors.consequence: The prediction gives nonzero Foucault precession at the equator.

commonErrors.description: Reverses one Coriolis sign so both horizontal equations have the same coupling direction.
commonErrors.consequence: The complex reduction no longer represents a rotating oscillation plane.

problems.flawedProof: Earth's full angular speed rotates every pendulum plane, so $T_F=2\pi/\Omega=23.93\,\mathrm h$ at all latitudes. Both equations contain $+2\Omega\dot y$ and $+2\Omega\dot x$, giving counterclockwise precession everywhere.

problems.title: The Eötvös correction distinguishes eastbound and westbound apparent weight
problems.objective: Radial kinematics and Coriolis acceleration derive the signed Eötvös correction relative to stationary local gravity and quantify its directional asymmetry.
problems.statement:
At latitude $\lambda$, let $g_0$ be the apparent downward gravitational acceleration measured by an observer stationary on a spherical rotating Earth; it already includes the stationary centrifugal correction. A vehicle moves due east at signed ground speed $v$ along a parallel of local curvature radius approximated by Earth radius $R$.

Derive the leading change in apparent downward acceleration relative to the stationary value,
$$
\Delta g_{\rm down}=-2\Omega v\cos\lambda-\frac{v^2}{R},
$$
clearly separating the signed Coriolis term from the curvature term. Explain the convention for westward motion and why adding the stationary centrifugal acceleration again would double count.

For $\lambda=30.0^\circ$, $|v|=250\,\mathrm{m/s}$, $\Omega=7.2921159\times10^{-5}\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$, $R=6.371\times10^6\,\mathrm m$, and vehicle mass $80.0\,\mathrm{kg}$, compute the apparent-weight change for eastbound and westbound travel and their difference. Check $v\to0$ and reversal of direction.
permittedResults: A path of speed $|v|$ on a circle of radius $R$ requires inward normal acceleration $v^2/R$.
problems.strategy: Work relative to the already rotating stationary observer, project the velocity-dependent Coriolis term vertically, then add the direction-independent path-curvature requirement before converting acceleration change to normal-force change.
hints: With east velocity $v\hat{\mathbf x}$, the upward component of $-2\boldsymbol\Omega\times\mathbf v$ is $2\Omega v\cos\lambda$.
An upward inertial contribution decreases the supporting normal force required for a fixed-altitude path.
Use signed $v$ in the linear term but $v^2$ in the curvature term.
problems.solution:
In east-north-up axes,
$\boldsymbol\Omega=(0,\Omega\cos\lambda,\Omega\sin\lambda)$ and
$\mathbf v=(v,0,0)$. Therefore
$$
(-2\boldsymbol\Omega\times\mathbf v)_z
=2\Omega v\cos\lambda.
$$
For eastward motion this is upward and reduces the required support. In addition, the moving vehicle requires downward curvature acceleration $v^2/R$, also reducing its normal force relative to a stationary observer. Since $g_0$ already includes stationary centrifugal acceleration,
$$
\boxed{\Delta g_{\rm down}
=-2\Omega v\cos\lambda-\frac{v^2}{R}}.
$$
Westward travel is represented by $v<0$; only the Coriolis term reverses.

For $|v|=250\,\mathrm{m/s}$,
$$
2\Omega |v|\cos30^\circ
=0.03158\,\mathrm{m/s^2},
\qquad
\frac{v^2}{R}=0.009810\,\mathrm{m/s^2}.
$$
Thus eastbound
$$
\Delta g_E=-(0.03158+0.009810)
=-0.04139\,\mathrm{m/s^2},
$$
so
$\boxed{\Delta N_E=(80.0)\Delta g_E=-3.31\,\mathrm N}$.
Westbound,
$$
\Delta g_W=+0.03158-0.009810
=0.02177\,\mathrm{m/s^2},
$$
so
$\boxed{\Delta N_W=+1.74\,\mathrm N}$.
The west-minus-east difference is
$$
\boxed{\Delta N_W-\Delta N_E
=4m\Omega|v|\cos\lambda=5.05\,\mathrm N}.
$$
As $v\to0$, both changes vanish. Direction reversal flips the linear Eötvös contribution but leaves the curvature correction unchanged.
rubricCriteria: Projects the signed Coriolis acceleration onto the local vertical without re-adding stationary centrifugal gravity.
Combines direction-sensitive rotation and direction-insensitive path curvature with the correct normal-force sign.
Computes eastbound, westbound, and difference values and verifies zero-speed and reversal limits.

commonErrors.description: Uses $v^2$ in the Coriolis contribution so east and west give the same effect.
commonErrors.consequence: The defining directional Eötvös asymmetry disappears.

commonErrors.description: Adds Earth's stationary centrifugal correction to $g_0$ a second time.
commonErrors.consequence: The baseline apparent weight is shifted even when vehicle speed tends to zero.

problems.flawedProof: Both rotation and path curvature depend on $v^2$, so eastbound and westbound vehicles have the same weight change. Adding stationary centrifugal acceleration gives a nonzero correction even at $v=0$.

problems.title: The inertia tensor rate records the symmetric position-velocity moment
problems.objective: Inertia-tensor differentiation captures fixed-axis reorientation even when all pair distances are instantaneously constant.
problems.statement: For particles relative to their barycenter define $I_{ab}=\sum_i m_i(\rho_i^2\delta_{ab}-\rho_{i,a}\rho_{i,b})$. Derive $\dot I_{ab}$. Evaluate $\dot I$ for two $1.00\,\mathrm{kg}$ particles with $\boldsymbol\rho_1=(1.00,0,0)\,\mathrm m$, $\boldsymbol\rho_2=(-1.00,0,0)\,\mathrm m$, $\dot{\boldsymbol\rho}_1=(0,2.00,0)\,\mathrm{m/s}$, and $\dot{\boldsymbol\rho}_2=(0,-2.00,0)\,\mathrm{m/s}$. Explain why constant interparticle distance does not imply a constant inertia tensor in fixed axes.
permittedResults: Differentiate tensor components with the ordinary product rule.
The Kronecker delta $\delta_{ab}$ is constant.
problems.strategy: First: Differentiate both $\rho_i^2$ and the dyadic product $\rho_{i,a}\rho_{i,b}$. Next: Compute the two particles' contributions before adding them. Finally: Interpret off-diagonal rates as reorientation and check units $\mathrm{kg\,m^2/s}$.
hints: Differentiate both $\rho_i^2$ and the dyadic product $\rho_{i,a}\rho_{i,b}$.
Compute the two particles' contributions before adding them.
Interpret off-diagonal rates as reorientation and check units $\mathrm{kg\,m^2/s}$.
problems.solution:
Product differentiation gives
$\boxed{\dot I_{ab}=\sum_i m_i[2(\boldsymbol\rho_i\cdot\dot{\boldsymbol\rho}_i)\delta_{ab}-\dot\rho_{i,a}\rho_{i,b}-\rho_{i,a}\dot\rho_{i,b}]}$.
Here each dot product is zero. Particle 1 contributes $-(\dot\rho\rho^T+\rho\dot\rho^T)$ with $xy$ and $yx$ entries $-2$; particle 2 contributes the same. Thus
$\boxed{\dot I=\begin{pmatrix}0&-4&0\\-4&0&0\\0&0&0\end{pmatrix}\,\mathrm{kg\,m^2/s}}$.
The separation magnitude is instantaneously constant because relative position and velocity are perpendicular, but the line joining the particles is rotating, so its tensor components in fixed axes change. In a co-rotating principal frame the same rigid shape has constant principal moments.
rubricCriteria: Differentiates both $\rho_i^2$ and the dyadic product $\rho_{i,a}\rho_{i,b}$.
Computes the two particles' contributions before adding them.
Interprets off-diagonal rates as reorientation and check units $\mathrm{kg\,m^2/s}$.

commonErrors.description: Differentiates only the scalar-radius term.
commonErrors.consequence: Tensor reorientation terms disappear, erasing the nonzero off-diagonal inertia rate.

commonErrors.description: Cancels the two particles because their positions are opposite.
commonErrors.consequence: The position-velocity dyadics are even under simultaneous sign reversal and actually add.

problems.flawedProof: Opposite positions make all tensor rates cancel, so $\dot I=0$. Since the separation length is constant, every fixed-axis inertia component must also be constant.

problems.title: Equal and opposite noncentral forces conserve momentum but create a spin couple
problems.objective: Noncentral action-reaction forces conserve linear momentum yet generate the correct pure-couple torque.
problems.statement: Two particles are at $\mathbf r_1=(a,0,0)$ and $\mathbf r_2=(-a,0,0)$ and experience internal forces $\mathbf F_1=(0,F,0)$ and $\mathbf F_2=-\mathbf F_1$. Compute the rates of total linear and angular momentum about the origin. For $a=0.400\,\mathrm m$ and $F=5.00\,\mathrm N$, find the couple torque. Explain why this force law violates the central-force hypothesis even though it obeys equal-and-opposite action and reaction, and state the $a\to0$ limit.
permittedResults: $\dot{\mathbf P}=\sum_i\mathbf F_i$.
$\dot{\mathbf L}=\sum_i\mathbf r_i\times\mathbf F_i$.
problems.strategy: First: Add the forces before evaluating any torques. Next: Compute both position-force cross products with the right-hand rule. Finally: Relate the surviving couple to the separation vector and audit the zero-arm limit.
hints: Add the forces before evaluating any torques.
Compute both position-force cross products with the right-hand rule.
Relate the surviving couple to the separation vector and audit the zero-arm limit.
problems.solution:
The resultant is $\mathbf F_1+\mathbf F_2=0$, so $\boxed{\dot{\mathbf P}=0}$. The torque is
$\boldsymbol\tau=(a,0,0)\times(0,F,0)+(-a,0,0)\times(0,-F,0)=2aF\hat z$.
Numerically, $\boxed{\dot L_z=2(0.400)(5.00)=4.00\,\mathrm{N\,m}}$. The forces are perpendicular to the line joining the particles, not parallel to it; Newton's third-law pairing therefore cancels translation but produces a pure internal couple. As $a\to0$ at fixed $F$, the moment arm and torque vanish. A physically closed particle model would need additional internal degrees of freedom carrying the compensating angular momentum.
rubricCriteria: Adds the forces before evaluating any torques.
Computes both position-force cross products with the right-hand rule.
Relates the surviving couple to the separation vector and audit the zero-arm limit.

commonErrors.description: Cancels equal-and-opposite forces before taking moments about their different application points.
commonErrors.consequence: It incorrectly sets the couple torque to zero.

commonErrors.description: Computes only one force's torque.
commonErrors.consequence: The couple magnitude is underestimated by a factor of two.

problems.flawedProof: Since the forces sum to zero, both $\dot{\mathbf P}$ and $\dot{\mathbf L}$ vanish. Equal-and-opposite action and reaction always conserve particle angular momentum.

problems.title: A velocity jump is the distributional signature of an impulse
problems.objective: Distributional integration and triangular regularization give the same finite velocity jump and continuous position.
problems.statement: A particle obeys $m\dot v=F_{\rm reg}(t)+J\delta(t-t_0)$, where $F_{\rm reg}$ is bounded near $t_0$. Derive the exact velocity jump by integrating over a shrinking interval. Then let $F_\epsilon(t)=J(1-|t-t_0|/\epsilon)/\epsilon$ for $|t-t_0|<\epsilon$ and zero otherwise. Verify its impulse and show its velocity change tends to the same jump. For $m=2.50\,\mathrm{kg}$, $J=-7.50\,\mathrm{N\,s}$, and $v(t_0^-)=4.00\,\mathrm{m/s}$, find $v(t_0^+)$.
permittedResults: The Dirac delta integrates to one across its support point.
A bounded function has vanishing integral over an interval whose width tends to zero.
problems.strategy: First: Integrate Newton's equation from $t_0-\eta$ to $t_0+\eta$ before taking $\eta\to0$. Next: Compute the area of the symmetric triangular regularization. Finally: Apply the signed momentum jump and verify that a negative impulse reduces velocity.
hints: Integrate Newton's equation from $t_0-\eta$ to $t_0+\eta$ before taking $\eta\to0$.
Compute the area of the symmetric triangular regularization.
Apply the signed momentum jump and verify that a negative impulse reduces velocity.
problems.solution:
Integration gives
$m[v(t_0+\eta)-v(t_0-\eta)]=\int F_{\rm reg}dt+J$.
The regular integral vanishes as $\eta\to0$, so $\boxed{m(v^+-v^-)=J}$. The regularized pulse is a triangle of base $2\epsilon$ and height $J/\epsilon$, hence area $J$; its integrated velocity change is exactly $J/m$ once the full pulse is included, converging to the same discontinuity as its support shrinks. Numerically,
$v^+=4.00+(-7.50)/2.50=\boxed{1.00\,\mathrm{m/s}}$.
The position remains continuous because a finite velocity jump integrated over zero duration gives no position jump.
rubricCriteria: Integrates Newton's equation from $t_0-\eta$ to $t_0+\eta$ before taking $\eta\to0$.
Computes the area of the symmetric triangular regularization.
Applies the signed momentum jump and verify that a negative impulse reduces velocity.

commonErrors.description: Treats the delta coefficient $J$ as a force rather than an impulse.
commonErrors.consequence: The jump has incorrect dimensions and depends on an arbitrary duration.

commonErrors.description: Uses the triangular pulse height as its area.
commonErrors.consequence: It introduces a spurious inverse-width factor.

problems.flawedProof: The delta force acts for zero time, so its impulse is zero and velocity is continuous. The triangular approximation has impulse $J/\epsilon$ and diverges as $\epsilon\to0$.

problems.title: A gravity gradient exerts a quadrupole torque on an extended system
problems.objective: Gravity-gradient expansion produces the dumbbell quadrupole torque, stable eigenvector alignment, and isotropic limit.
problems.statement: Two equal point masses $m$ form a dumbbell with offsets $\boldsymbol\rho_\pm=\pm(\ell/2)\mathbf n$ from the barycenter. In a linear external field $\mathbf g(\mathbf R+\boldsymbol\rho)=\mathbf g(\mathbf R)+T\boldsymbol\rho$, derive the leading torque about the barycenter. In the $xy$ plane take symmetric $T=\operatorname{diag}(2\alpha,-\alpha,0)$ and $\mathbf n=(\cos\theta,\sin\theta,0)$. Find $\tau_z(\theta)$ and the stable orientations if potential energy exists. Evaluate the maximum torque for $m=4.00\,\mathrm{kg}$, $\ell=2.00\,\mathrm m$, and $\alpha=0.500\,\mathrm{s^{-2}}$.
permittedResults: Uniform field terms have zero torque about the barycenter.
For symmetric $T$, the tidal potential is $-\sum_i m_i\boldsymbol\rho_i^TT\boldsymbol\rho_i/2$.
problems.strategy: First: Sum $m\boldsymbol\rho\times T\boldsymbol\rho$ for the two equal offsets. Next: Insert the planar unit vector and simplify with $\sin2\theta$. Finally: Use the tidal potential or torque slope to classify alignment and verify torque units.
hints: Sum $m\boldsymbol\rho\times T\boldsymbol\rho$ for the two equal offsets.
Insert the planar unit vector and simplify with $\sin2\theta$.
Use the tidal potential or torque slope to classify alignment and verify torque units.
problems.solution:
The uniform term cancels because $\sum m\boldsymbol\rho=0$. Both offsets give the same cross product, so
$\boldsymbol\tau=2m(\ell\mathbf n/2)\times T(\ell\mathbf n/2)=\tfrac12m\ell^2\mathbf n\times T\mathbf n$.
Here $(\mathbf n\times T\mathbf n)_z=\cos\theta(-\alpha\sin\theta)-\sin\theta(2\alpha\cos\theta)=-(3\alpha/2)\sin2\theta$. Thus
$\boxed{\tau_z=-(3m\ell^2\alpha/4)\sin2\theta}$.
The potential is minimized when the dumbbell aligns with the largest eigenvalue, the $x$ axis; the $y$ alignment is unstable. Maximum magnitude is $3m\ell^2\alpha/4=3(4)(4)(0.5)/4=\boxed{6.00\,\mathrm{N\,m}}$. If $T$ becomes isotropic, $T\mathbf n$ is parallel to $\mathbf n$ and torque vanishes.
rubricCriteria: Sums $m\boldsymbol\rho\times T\boldsymbol\rho$ for the two equal offsets.
Inserts the planar unit vector and simplify with $\sin2\theta$.
Uses the tidal potential or torque slope to classify alignment and verify torque units.

commonErrors.description: Keeps a torque from the uniform field at the barycenter.
commonErrors.consequence: It violates the defining zero first mass moment of barycentric offsets.

commonErrors.description: Drops one of the two equal dumbbell contributions.
commonErrors.consequence: The gravity-gradient torque is underestimated by a factor of two.

problems.flawedProof: The opposite offsets produce opposite tidal torques, so the total is zero for every orientation. A symmetric gravity gradient cannot orient a dumbbell.

problems.title: Time-varying damping contracts Newtonian phase volume by an exact history factor
problems.objective: Nonautonomous phase-flow divergence converts a time-dependent drag history into an exact Jacobian contraction and recovers conservative volume preservation only as a limit.
problems.statement:
In $d$ spatial dimensions consider
$$
\dot{\mathbf r}=\mathbf v,
\qquad
\dot{\mathbf v}=\frac1m\mathbf F(\mathbf r,t)-\frac{\gamma(t)}m\mathbf v,
$$
where $\mathbf F$ is velocity independent and $\gamma(t)\ge0$. Derive the divergence of this explicitly time-dependent $2d$-dimensional vector field. If $\mathcal J(t)$ is the determinant of the flow derivative with respect to initial phase-space data, derive the exact equation and solution for $\mathcal J(t)$ rather than assuming a constant contraction rate.

Specialize to
$$
\gamma(t)=\frac{\gamma_0}{1+t/T},
\qquad t\ge0,
$$
and obtain the phase-volume factor. For $d=3$, $m=2.00\,\mathrm{kg}$, $\gamma_0=0.400\,\mathrm{kg/s}$, $T=5.00\,\mathrm s$, and $t=10.0\,\mathrm s$, compute the factor.

Explain why explicit time dependence does not invalidate the Jacobian argument, why an arbitrary velocity-independent force does not change the result, and how the limits $\gamma_0\to0$ and $T\to\infty$ at fixed $t$ connect to conservative flow and constant linear drag.
permittedResults: For a differentiable nonautonomous flow, the Jacobian determinant obeys $d(\ln\mathcal J)/dt=\nabla\cdot\mathbf f$ along the trajectory.
problems.strategy: Take phase divergence with position and velocity coordinates treated independently, integrate the resulting scalar Jacobian equation along time, and postpone specialization of the drag history until after the general determinant formula is established.
hints: Differentiate each position-flow component with respect to its matching position coordinate, not with respect to velocity.
Each of the $d$ velocity derivatives contributes $-\gamma(t)/m$.
Integrate $\int_0^t\gamma_0(1+s/T)^{-1}ds=\gamma_0T\ln(1+t/T)$.
problems.solution:
The phase-space vector field is
$$
\mathbf f(\mathbf r,\mathbf v,t)
=\left(\mathbf v,\frac{\mathbf F(\mathbf r,t)}m
-\frac{\gamma(t)}m\mathbf v\right).
$$
Its divergence is
$$
\nabla_{(r,v)}\cdot\mathbf f
=\sum_{a=1}^d\frac{\partial v_a}{\partial r_a}
+\sum_{a=1}^d\frac{\partial}{\partial v_a}
\left(\frac{F_a}{m}-\frac{\gamma(t)}m v_a\right)
=\boxed{-\frac{d\gamma(t)}m}.
$$
The velocity-independent force contributes no velocity derivative, even if it varies with position and time.

The flow Jacobian therefore obeys
$$
\frac{d}{dt}\ln\mathcal J(t)=-\frac d m\gamma(t),
\qquad \mathcal J(0)=1,
$$
so
$$
\boxed{\mathcal J(t)=
\exp\left[-\frac d m\int_0^t\gamma(s)\,ds\right]}.
$$
This is a nonautonomous flow statement; explicit time dependence merely makes the accumulated divergence time dependent.

For the stated drag history,
$$
\boxed{\mathcal J(t)=(1+t/T)^{-d\gamma_0T/m}}.
$$
Here
$$
\frac{d\gamma_0T}{m}
=\frac{3(0.400)(5.00)}{2.00}=3,
$$
and $1+t/T=3$, giving
$$
\boxed{\mathcal J(10.0\,\mathrm s)=3^{-3}=\frac1{27}=0.03704}.
$$
As $\gamma_0\to0$, $\mathcal J\to1$, recovering velocity-independent conservative Newtonian phase-volume preservation. As $T\to\infty$ at fixed $t$, $\gamma(t)\to\gamma_0$ and
$\mathcal J\to e^{-d\gamma_0t/m}$, the constant-drag contraction factor.
rubricCriteria: Computes the nonautonomous phase divergence with one drag contribution per velocity dimension.
Integrates the Jacobian equation for a general drag history before specializing its time dependence.
Evaluates the power-law contraction and verifies conservative and constant-drag limits.

commonErrors.description: Uses $\partial\dot r_a/\partial v_a=1$ in a divergence that requires matching coordinate derivatives.
commonErrors.consequence: A spurious positive term makes even undamped Newtonian phase flow expand.

commonErrors.description: Substitutes the initial drag coefficient as a constant throughout the Jacobian exponential.
commonErrors.consequence: The exact logarithmic drag history and resulting power-law contraction are replaced by the wrong exponential.

problems.flawedProof: The divergence includes $\partial\dot r_a/\partial v_a=1$, so it is $d-d\gamma_0/m$ and remains constant even though $\gamma(t)$ changes. Thus $\mathcal J=e^{(d-d\gamma_0/m)t}$.

problems.title: Accretion in an accelerating frame requires both flux momentum and inertial force
problems.objective: Variable-mass balance in an accelerating frame tracks incoming momentum, inertial reaction, frame-relative speed, and inelastic energy loss without mixing frames.
problems.statement:
A cart moves along a frictionless inertial $x$ axis while continuously and perfectly inelastically capturing dust. Its mass is $m(t)=m_0+\alpha t$ with $m_0>0$ and $\alpha>0$. Before capture, every dust element is at rest in the inertial frame. A translating frame $S'$ has origin $X(t)=At^2/2$, where $A>0$, and $x'=x-X$. At $t=0$ the two frame origins are instantaneously at rest relative to each other, and the cart has $v'(0)=v_0$.

Derive the inertial open-system momentum equation from a capture during $dt$; do not assume that zero physical force implies $m\dot v=0$. Transform the result to $S'$, keeping separate the dust velocity measured in $S'$ and the fictitious force. Solve exactly for $v'(t)$ and verify the answer by reconstructing inertial momentum.

For $m_0=4.00\,\mathrm{kg}$, $\alpha=0.500\,\mathrm{kg/s}$, $v_0=3.00\,\mathrm{m/s}$, $A=1.20\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$, and $t=4.00\,\mathrm s$, compute $m$, the inertial cart speed, the frame speed, and $v'$. Compute the inertial kinetic-energy change of the accumulated cart and explain its sign. Audit the limits $A\to0$ and $\alpha\to0$, and state why inserting a zero incident speed directly in $S'$ is inconsistent.
permittedResults: During perfectly inelastic capture, momentum of the cart plus the incoming mass is balanced before and after the infinitesimal event.
For $x=x'+X(t)$, velocities and accelerations satisfy $v=v'+\dot X$ and $\dot v=\dot v'+\ddot X$.
problems.strategy: Balance momentum in the inertial frame over one capture event. Transform both the cart and incident-dust velocities into the accelerating coordinates. Solve through the conserved inertial momentum, then use limiting cases to expose any frame mismatch.
hints: Write $mv+u\,dm=(m+dm)(v+dv)$ with inertial dust speed $u=0$ before discarding second-order terms.
In $S'$, the incident dust speed is $u'=-At$, not zero, and the cart experiences fictitious force $-mA$.
Check the solution by showing that $m(t)[v'(t)+At]=m_0v_0$ for every time.
problems.solution:
For an incident inertial speed $u$, momentum balance during capture is
$mv+u\,dm=(m+dm)(v+dv)$. To first order,
$$
m\,dv=(u-v)\,dm,
\qquad
m\dot v=(u-v)\dot m.
$$
Here $u=0$ and $\dot m=\alpha$, so $d(mv)/dt=0$ and
$$
\boxed{m(t)v(t)=m_0v_0},
\qquad
v(t)=\frac{m_0v_0}{m_0+\alpha t}.
$$

Because $v=v'+At$ and $\dot v=\dot v'+A$, the incident dust has $u'=u-At=-At$. Transforming the open-system equation gives
$$
\boxed{m\dot v'=-mA+\alpha(u'-v')
=-mA+\alpha(-At-v')}.
$$
The two terms have distinct origins: $-mA$ is the fictitious force on the accumulated cart, while $\alpha(u'-v')$ is momentum flux relative to it. Reconstruction from the conserved inertial momentum gives
$$
\boxed{v'(t)=\frac{m_0v_0}{m_0+\alpha t}-At}.
$$
Direct differentiation verifies the transformed equation, and $m(v'+At)=m_0v_0$ verifies the invariant inertial ledger.

At $t=4.00\,\mathrm s$,
$$
m=4.00+(0.500)(4.00)=\boxed{6.00\,\mathrm{kg}},
\quad
v=\frac{(4.00)(3.00)}{6.00}=\boxed{2.00\,\mathrm{m/s}},
$$
while the frame origin has $\dot X=At=\boxed{4.80\,\mathrm{m/s}}$. Hence
$$
\boxed{v'=2.00-4.80=-2.80\,\mathrm{m/s}}.
$$
The accumulated-cart kinetic energy changes from
$K_0=\tfrac12(4.00)(3.00)^2=18.0\,\mathrm J$ to
$K=\tfrac12(6.00)(2.00)^2=12.0\,\mathrm J$, so
$$
\boxed{\Delta K=-6.00\,\mathrm J}.
$$
The missing mechanical energy is dissipated in the perfectly inelastic captures; momentum conservation does not imply kinetic-energy conservation.

When $A\to0$, $S'$ becomes inertial and $v'=m_0v_0/m$. When $\alpha\to0$, no mass enters and $v'=v_0-At$, the usual description of free inertial motion in an accelerating frame. Setting $u'=0$ would assert that the dust co-moves with the accelerating frame, contradicting its stated inertial rest and destroying the transformed momentum balance.
rubricCriteria: Balances each infinitesimal capture with the incoming inertial dust momentum and obtains $m\dot v=(u-v)\dot m$.
Transforms cart and dust velocities consistently, retaining both $-mA$ and $\alpha(u'-v')$ in the $S'$ equation.
Reconstructs constant inertial momentum, computes $v'=-2.80\,\mathrm{m/s}$ and $\Delta K=-6.00\,\mathrm J$, and checks both limits.

commonErrors.description: Sets the incident dust speed to zero in the accelerating frame because it is zero in the inertial frame.
commonErrors.consequence: The momentum-flux term is assigned to the wrong material stream and the transformed speed no longer reconstructs constant inertial momentum.

commonErrors.description: Uses only the fictitious force or only the mass-flux term after changing frames.
commonErrors.consequence: One source of frame-relative momentum change is lost, giving a result that fails either the $A\to0$ or $\alpha\to0$ limit.

problems.flawedProof: The dust is stationary, so $u'=0$ in every coordinate system. With no physical horizontal force, the accelerating-frame equation is $m\dot v'=-mA$, giving $v'=v_0-At=-1.80\,\mathrm{m/s}$ at four seconds; changing mass does not enter.

problems.title: A restitution impact map has a complementarity boundary and a measurable Jacobian
problems.objective: Impulse complementarity separates approaching from separating states, while center-of-mass coordinates reveal restitution contraction and energy loss exactly.
problems.statement:
Two particles move on a line with masses $m_1,m_2>0$ and nonpenetration gap $g=x_2-x_1\ge0$. At a contact event define relative normal velocity $w=v_2-v_1$. A compressive impulse $J\ge0$ changes velocities by
$$
v_1^+=v_1^- -\frac{J}{m_1},
\qquad
v_2^+=v_2^- +\frac{J}{m_2}.
$$
For an approaching impact $w^-<0$, impose Newton restitution $w^+=-e w^-$ with $0\le e\le1$. Derive $J$, the post-impact map, and the kinetic-energy loss. State the no-impact branch when bodies are separating and formulate the positional complementarity condition without confusing it with restitution.

Transform the velocity map to total momentum $P$ and relative velocity $w$ and compute its Jacobian determinant. Interpret the cases $e=1$ and $e=0$.

For $m_1=2.00\,\mathrm{kg}$, $m_2=3.00\,\mathrm{kg}$, $v_1^-=4.00\,\mathrm{m/s}$, $v_2^-=-1.00\,\mathrm{m/s}$, and $e=0.600$, compute $J$, both outgoing velocities, and energy loss.
permittedResults: The reduced mass satisfies $\mu^{-1}=m_1^{-1}+m_2^{-1}$.
problems.strategy: Solve restitution in the scalar relative coordinate, preserve total momentum separately, and use the invertible change from particle velocities to $(P,w)$ to read the map determinant and energy change.
hints: The impulse changes relative velocity by $J(1/m_1+1/m_2)$.
At contact, use $J\ge0$, $g\ge0$, and $Jg=0$; also require approach before applying an impact impulse.
Relative kinetic energy in the center-of-mass frame is $\mu w^2/2$.
problems.solution:
The relative jump is
$$
w^+=w^-+J\left(\frac1{m_1}+\frac1{m_2}\right)
=w^-+\frac J\mu.
$$
For $w^-<0$, restitution gives
$$
\boxed{J=-\mu(1+e)w^-}>0.
$$
The stated velocity updates then define the post-impact map. If $g=0$ but $w^-\ge0$, the particles are separating or tangent and the admissible branch is $J=0$; restitution is not applied to create an attractive impulse. The positional contact law is
$$
\boxed{g\ge0,\qquad J\ge0,\qquad Jg=0},
$$
supplemented at an instantaneous collision by the approach and restitution rules.

In coordinates $(P,w)$,
$$
\boxed{P^+=P^-},
\qquad
\boxed{w^+=-e w^-}.
$$
Therefore the velocity-map Jacobian determinant is
$$
\boxed{\det D\Phi=-e}.
$$
For $e=1$ the map preserves phase-volume magnitude and reverses the relative direction; for $e=0$ it collapses all incoming relative speeds to $w^+=0$, so the map is noninvertible. The energy loss is
$$
\boxed{K^- -K^+=\frac12\mu(1-e^2)(w^-)^2}.
$$

Numerically, $\mu=(2\cdot3)/5=1.20\,\mathrm{kg}$ and $w^-=-5.00\,\mathrm{m/s}$, hence
$$
J=(1.20)(1.600)(5.00)=\boxed{9.60\,\mathrm{N\,s}}.
$$
Thus
$$
\boxed{v_1^+=4.00-9.60/2.00=-0.800\,\mathrm{m/s}},
$$
$$
\boxed{v_2^+=-1.00+9.60/3.00=2.20\,\mathrm{m/s}}.
$$
Their relative speed is $3.00\,\mathrm{m/s}=-e w^-$, and
$$
K^- -K^+=\frac12(1.20)(1-0.36)(25.0)
=\boxed{9.60\,\mathrm J}.
$$
rubricCriteria: Derives the positive impulse on the approach branch and states the zero-impulse separating branch.
Separates positional complementarity from the restitution law and preserves total momentum.
Computes the determinant, its endpoint interpretations, and all numerical velocities and energy loss.

commonErrors.description: Applies restitution to a separating state and permits a negative contact impulse.
commonErrors.consequence: The unilateral contact becomes adhesive and pulls bodies back together.

commonErrors.description: Reports Jacobian magnitude one for every restitution coefficient because momentum is conserved.
commonErrors.consequence: Contraction of the relative-velocity direction and the singular perfectly inelastic map are missed.

problems.flawedProof: Momentum conservation makes every collision map volume preserving, so $\det D\Phi=1$. The same restitution formula applies for $w^->0$, producing a negative impulse that restores contact.

problems.title: Galilean boost symmetry carries a conserved center-of-mass charge
problems.objective: Boost-charge conservation fixes the center-of-mass worldline intercept and its transformations independently of momentum.
problems.statement: For an isolated Newtonian particle system with total momentum $\mathbf P$ and total mass $M$, define the boost charge $\mathbf K=\sum_i m_i\mathbf r_i-t\mathbf P$. Prove directly that $\mathbf K$ is constant and show how it transforms under an origin translation and a Galilean boost. Use it with $M=12.0\,\mathrm{kg}$, $\mathbf P=(6.00,-3.00)\,\mathrm{kg\,m/s}$, and $\mathbf K=(24.0,12.0)\,\mathrm{kg\,m}$ to find the barycenter at $t=8.00\,\mathrm s$. Explain why this conserved vector is independent of, but compatible with, momentum conservation.
permittedResults: For an isolated system, $\dot{\mathbf P}=0$.
$\sum_i m_i\mathbf r_i=M\mathbf R$.
problems.strategy: First: Differentiate the proposed charge using both barycenter and momentum balances. Next: Apply $\mathbf r'=\mathbf r-\mathbf a-\mathbf U t$ consistently to positions and momentum. Finally: Solve $M\mathbf R=\mathbf K+t\mathbf P$ and audit dimensions.
hints: Differentiate the proposed charge using both barycenter and momentum balances.
Apply $\mathbf r'=\mathbf r-\mathbf a-\mathbf U t$ consistently to positions and momentum.
Solve $M\mathbf R=\mathbf K+t\mathbf P$ and audit dimensions.
problems.solution:
Differentiating gives $\dot{\mathbf K}=\sum_i m_i\mathbf v_i-\mathbf P-t\dot{\mathbf P}=0$. Hence $M\mathbf R=\mathbf K+t\mathbf P$. Under a constant origin shift $\mathbf a$, $\mathbf K' =\mathbf K-M\mathbf a$. Under a boost $\mathbf U$ with unchanged origin at $t=0$, $\mathbf r_i'=\mathbf r_i-\mathbf U t$ and $\mathbf P'=\mathbf P-M\mathbf U$, so $\mathbf K'=\sum m_i(\mathbf r_i-\mathbf U t)-t(\mathbf P-M\mathbf U)=\mathbf K$. Numerically,
$\mathbf R(8)=[(24,12)+8(6,-3)]/12=(72,-12)/12=\boxed{(6.00,-1.00)\,\mathrm m}$.
Momentum fixes barycenter velocity; $\mathbf K$ fixes its intercept. The two constants together specify the full inertial barycenter worldline.
rubricCriteria: Differentiates the proposed charge using both barycenter and momentum balances.
Applies $\mathbf r'=\mathbf r-\mathbf a-\mathbf U t$ consistently to positions and momentum.
Solves $M\mathbf R=\mathbf K+t\mathbf P$ and audit dimensions.

commonErrors.description: Omits the time-times-momentum term when defining the boost charge.
commonErrors.consequence: Boost-charge truncation leaves a quantity that drifts with barycenter momentum.

commonErrors.description: Transforms positions under a boost but leaves momentum unchanged.
commonErrors.consequence: Boost transformation inconsistency makes the conserved intercept appear frame dependent.

problems.flawedProof: The conserved boost charge is $M\mathbf R+t\mathbf P$. It is invariant because both terms grow together, giving $\mathbf R(8)=(-2.00,3.00)\,\mathrm m$.

problems.title: Two-stage rocket performance has an interior propellant-allocation optimum
problems.objective: Serial staging calculus allocates a fixed propellant inventory between unequal exhaust speeds and dry masses, including boundary and second-derivative checks.
problems.statement:
An ideal two-stage rocket operates impulsively with no gravity or drag. Payload mass is $L$. Stage 1 has dry mass $s_1$, exhaust speed $c_1$, and propellant $p_1$; after its burn, its dry mass is discarded. Stage 2 has dry mass $s_2$, exhaust speed $c_2$, and propellant $p_2$. The total propellant inventory is fixed: $p_1+p_2=P$, with both allocations nonnegative.

Derive the total ideal velocity increment as a function of $p_2$. Find the interior stationary allocation, give the condition under which it lies in $0<p_2<P$, and use the second derivative or derivative sign to decide whether it is a maximum. Compare both boundary allocations.

For
$$
L=1000\,\mathrm{kg},\quad s_1=400\,\mathrm{kg},\quad
s_2=200\,\mathrm{kg},\quad P=3000\,\mathrm{kg},
$$
$$
c_1=4.00\,\mathrm{km/s},\qquad c_2=3.50\,\mathrm{km/s},
$$
compute the optimal $p_1,p_2$ and total $\Delta v$. Evaluate $\Delta v$ at $p_2=0$ and $p_2=P$. State why this mathematical optimum depends on the idealized fixed-dry-mass assumptions.
permittedResults: An ideal burn with exhaust speed $c$ gives $\Delta v=c\ln(m_{\rm before}/m_{\rm after})$.
problems.strategy: Write each burn's before-and-after mass while retaining all downstream hardware during stage 1. Eliminate $p_1=P-p_2$, differentiate the two logarithms, and compare an admissible stationary point with both allocation boundaries.
hints: Let $B=L+s_1+s_2$ and $C=L+s_2$; the stage-1 initial mass is $B+P$.
Differentiate $c_1[\ln(B+P)-\ln(B+p_2)]+c_2[\ln(C+p_2)-\ln C]$.
A stationary point is not sufficient until it lies within the propellant interval and beats or is classified relative to both endpoints.
problems.solution:
During stage 1, all payload and stage-2 mass remain aboard. Thus
$$
\Delta v_1=c_1\ln\frac{L+s_1+s_2+P}{L+s_1+s_2+p_2}.
$$
After stage-1 dry mass is discarded, stage 2 gives
$$
\Delta v_2=c_2\ln\frac{L+s_2+p_2}{L+s_2}.
$$
With $B=L+s_1+s_2$ and $C=L+s_2$,
$$
\boxed{\Delta v(p_2)=c_1\ln\frac{B+P}{B+p_2}
+c_2\ln\frac{C+p_2}{C}}.
$$
Differentiation gives
$$
\Delta v'=-\frac{c_1}{B+p_2}+\frac{c_2}{C+p_2}.
$$
For $c_1\ne c_2$, the stationary allocation is
$$
\boxed{p_2^*=\frac{c_1C-c_2B}{c_2-c_1}},
$$
provided $0<p_2^*<P$. At the numerical values, $B=1600\,\mathrm{kg}$, $C=1200\,\mathrm{kg}$, and
$$
p_2^*=\frac{(4.00)(1200)-(3.50)(1600)}{3.50-4.00}
=\boxed{1600\,\mathrm{kg}},
$$
so $\boxed{p_1^*=1400\,\mathrm{kg}}$. The second derivative is
$$
\Delta v''=\frac{c_1}{(B+p_2)^2}-\frac{c_2}{(C+p_2)^2},
$$
which is negative at $p_2^*$, confirming a local maximum; the endpoint comparison below makes it global on the interval.

The optimum gives
$$
\Delta v^*=4.00\ln\frac{4600}{3200}
+3.50\ln\frac{2800}{1200}
=\boxed{4.417\,\mathrm{km/s}}.
$$
At $p_2=0$,
$$
\Delta v=4.00\ln(4600/1600)=\boxed{4.224\,\mathrm{km/s}},
$$
while at $p_2=3000\,\mathrm{kg}$,
$$
\Delta v=3.50\ln(4200/1200)=\boxed{4.385\,\mathrm{km/s}}.
$$
The interior allocation is therefore best. Real dry mass, tankage, thrust, gravity loss, and exhaust performance depend on propellant and stage design; fixing $s_1,s_2,c_1,c_2$ while reallocating propellant is the explicit idealization behind this optimum.
rubricCriteria: Builds both stage mass ratios without prematurely discarding downstream or stage-1 dry mass.
Derives the admissible stationary allocation and verifies its maximum classification.
Computes the optimal and boundary velocity increments and states the model-dependence of the result.

commonErrors.description: Removes stage-2 propellant from the stage-1 initial or final mass ledger.
commonErrors.consequence: The first burn receives a fictitious mass ratio and the allocation derivative is wrong.

commonErrors.description: Accepts the stationary formula without checking interval bounds, curvature, or endpoints.
commonErrors.consequence: A minimum or inadmissible negative propellant allocation can be mislabeled optimal.

problems.flawedProof: Each stage sees only its own dry mass and propellant, so maximize $c_1\ln[(s_1+p_1)/s_1]+c_2\ln[(s_2+p_2)/s_2]$. Setting derivatives equal gives $p_1=p_2=1500\,\mathrm{kg}$ automatically, with no endpoint check.

problems.title: The equal-mass Euler line is a rigidly rotating three-body solution
problems.objective: Euler-line force geometry establishes the rigid rotation rate, middle-body consistency, and Keplerian scaling.
problems.statement: Three equal masses $m$ lie at positions $-a\hat{\mathbf x}$, $0$, and $+a\hat{\mathbf x}$ in a line through their barycenter. Show that this shape can rotate rigidly in a plane about the middle mass, and derive its angular speed. Check the middle mass equation explicitly. For $m=1.00\times10^{18}\,\mathrm{kg}$ and $a=2.00\times10^5\,\mathrm m$, compute the period. Compare the dimensional scaling with the equilateral relative equilibrium without claiming equal numerical coefficients.
permittedResults: The outer mass feels attractions from the middle mass at distance $a$ and the other outer mass at distance $2a$.
Rigid planar rotation requires inward acceleration $\omega^2a$.
problems.strategy: First: Add the two inward force contributions on one outer mass. Next: Verify that forces on the central mass cancel by symmetry. Finally: Solve for $\omega$ and evaluate the period with the $a^{3/2}/\sqrt{Gm}$ scaling.
hints: Add the two inward force contributions on one outer mass.
Verify that forces on the central mass cancel by symmetry.
Solve for $\omega$ and evaluate the period with the $a^{3/2}/\sqrt{Gm}$ scaling.
problems.solution:
An outer mass feels inward acceleration
$Gm/a^2+Gm/(2a)^2=(5/4)Gm/a^2$. Rigid rotation therefore requires
$\omega^2a=(5/4)Gm/a^2$, so $\boxed{\omega^2=5Gm/(4a^3)}$. The two attractions on the middle mass are equal and opposite; since it lies at the rotation center, its required acceleration is also zero. Numerically,
$\omega^2=5(6.6743\times10^{-11})(10^{18})/[4(2\times10^5)^3]=1.0429\times10^{-8}\,\mathrm{s^{-2}}$,
so $\omega=1.0212\times10^{-4}\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$ and $P=2\pi/\omega=\boxed{6.153\times10^4\,\mathrm s=17.09\,\mathrm h}$. Both Euler and equilateral configurations have Keplerian scaling, but geometry changes the dimensionless coefficient.
rubricCriteria: Adds the two inward force contributions on one outer mass.
Verifies that forces on the central mass cancel by symmetry.
Solves for $\omega$ and evaluate the period with the $a^{3/2}/\sqrt{Gm}$ scaling.

commonErrors.description: Omits the attraction between the two outer masses.
commonErrors.consequence: The angular speed is underestimated.

commonErrors.description: Requires the middle mass to have the same centripetal acceleration as an outer mass.
commonErrors.consequence: It assigns a nonzero rotation radius to the barycentric central mass.

problems.flawedProof: Only the nearest middle mass attracts an outer mass, giving $\omega^2=Gm/a^3$. The middle mass must also circle at radius $a$, so the configuration is inconsistent.

problems.title: Translation-invariant interactions cannot shift a common harmonic barycenter mode
problems.objective: Common harmonic confinement leaves an interaction-independent barycenter mode and exposes the failure under unequal frequencies.
problems.statement: Particles of masses $m_i$ interact through arbitrary translation-invariant pair potentials and also feel a common isotropic trap force $-m_i\Omega^2\mathbf r_i$. Prove that the barycenter obeys an exact oscillator equation independent of every interaction. For $\Omega=3.00\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$, $\mathbf R(0)=(0.400,-0.200)\,\mathrm m$, and $\dot{\mathbf R}(0)=(0.600,0)\,\mathrm{m/s}$, find $\mathbf R(t)$ and the maximum $x$ displacement. Then show precisely why unequal trap frequencies $\Omega_i$ destroy the closed barycenter equation.
permittedResults: Translation-invariant pair forces cancel in the total force.
The solution of $\ddot x+\Omega^2x=0$ is fixed by initial position and velocity.
problems.strategy: First: Sum the equations with mass weights and cancel all internal pairs. Next: Solve each barycenter component from the stated initial data. Finally: For unequal frequencies inspect the weighted trap sum and test whether it depends only on $\mathbf R$.
hints: Sum the equations with mass weights and cancel all internal pairs.
Solve each barycenter component from the stated initial data.
For unequal frequencies inspect the weighted trap sum and test whether it depends only on $\mathbf R$.
problems.solution:
Summation gives $M\ddot{\mathbf R}=-\Omega^2\sum_i m_i\mathbf r_i=-M\Omega^2\mathbf R$, hence
$\boxed{\ddot{\mathbf R}+\Omega^2\mathbf R=0}$ regardless of the interactions. Therefore
$R_x=0.400\cos3t+(0.600/3)\sin3t=0.400\cos3t+0.200\sin3t$ and $R_y=-0.200\cos3t$, in metres. The $x$ amplitude is $\sqrt{0.400^2+0.200^2}=\boxed{0.4472\,\mathrm m}$. With unequal frequencies, the trap resultant is $-\sum_i m_i\Omega_i^2\mathbf r_i$, which cannot generally be written as a constant times $M\mathbf R$; internal coordinates then couple into barycenter motion. If all $\Omega_i\to0$, uniform barycenter motion is recovered.
rubricCriteria: Sums the equations with mass weights and cancel all internal pairs.
Solves each barycenter component from the stated initial data.
Tests unequal-frequency confinement through the position-weighted force sum rather than a closed function of $\mathbf R$.

commonErrors.description: Lets internal interaction stiffness enter the barycenter frequency.
commonErrors.consequence: It fails to cancel equal-opposite translation-invariant pair forces.

commonErrors.description: Averages unequal frequencies rather than their position-weighted squared values.
commonErrors.consequence: It asserts a closed barycenter oscillator where none exists generally.

problems.flawedProof: The barycenter frequency is $\sqrt{\Omega^2+\sum k_{ij}/M}$ because every internal spring adds restoring force. Unequal trap frequencies can always be replaced by their arithmetic mean.

problems.title: Center-of-mass decomposition gives the sharp breakup-energy floor
problems.objective: Center-of-mass energy decomposition supplies the sharp breakup floor and the required internal kinetic excess.
problems.statement: A system of fragments with masses $m_i$ has fixed total momentum $\mathbf P$ after breakup. Prove that total kinetic energy satisfies $K\ge P^2/(2M)$ and characterize equality. If fragments have masses $1.00$, $2.00$, and $3.00\,\mathrm{kg}$ and total momentum $(6.00,8.00,0)\,\mathrm{kg\,m/s}$, find the sharp minimum kinetic energy. If an available post-breakup kinetic energy is $12.0\,\mathrm J$, decide whether the data are feasible and quantify the minimum internal kinetic energy above barycenter translation.
permittedResults: Write $\mathbf v_i=\mathbf V+\mathbf u_i$ with $\mathbf V=\mathbf P/M$ and $\sum_i m_i\mathbf u_i=0$.
problems.strategy: First: Expand kinetic energy about the barycenter velocity. Next: Use the zero mass-weighted residual-velocity sum to remove the cross term. Finally: Compare the numerical energy with the sharp translational floor rather than with zero.
hints: Expand kinetic energy about the barycenter velocity.
Use the zero mass-weighted residual-velocity sum to remove the cross term.
Compare the numerical energy with the sharp translational floor rather than with zero.
problems.solution:
With $\mathbf v_i=\mathbf V+\mathbf u_i$,
$K=\tfrac12M V^2+\mathbf V\cdot\sum_i m_i\mathbf u_i+\tfrac12\sum_i m_iu_i^2=\frac{P^2}{2M}+K_{\rm int}$,
where $K_{\rm int}\ge0$. Thus $\boxed{K\ge P^2/(2M)}$, with equality only when all fragments share velocity $\mathbf V$. Here $M=6.00\,\mathrm{kg}$ and $P^2=100\,\mathrm{kg^2m^2/s^2}$, so
$K_{\min}=100/12=\boxed{8.333\,\mathrm J}$. An available $12.0\,\mathrm J$ is feasible because it exceeds the floor; it requires $\boxed{K_{\rm int}=3.667\,\mathrm J}$ of relative motion. In the $\mathbf P\to0$ limit, the translational floor vanishes but internal kinetic energy may remain.
rubricCriteria: Expands kinetic energy about the barycenter velocity.
Uses the zero mass-weighted residual-velocity sum to remove the cross term.
Compares the numerical energy with the sharp translational floor rather than with zero.

commonErrors.description: Uses the largest fragment mass instead of total mass in the translational floor.
commonErrors.consequence: The feasibility threshold is not invariant under regrouping fragments.

commonErrors.description: Claims equality when momenta rather than velocities are equal.
commonErrors.consequence: Unequal masses would then retain relative motion and positive internal energy.

problems.flawedProof: The minimum is obtained by equal fragment momenta, giving $K_{\min}=P^2/[2(m_1^2+m_2^2+m_3^2)]=3.57\,\mathrm J$. Therefore nearly all of the $12.0\,\mathrm J$ is internal.

problems.title: Bounded force prevents a finite-time velocity blowup
problems.objective: Uniform force bounds give explicit finite-time speed and displacement estimates while excluding singular inverse-square misuse.
problems.statement: A particle of mass $m>0$ satisfies $m\ddot{\mathbf r}=\mathbf F(\mathbf r,t)$ on $0\le t<T$, and suppose $|\mathbf F|\le F_{\max}$ throughout the region visited. Prove explicit bounds on speed and displacement that exclude a finite-time velocity or position blowup before $T$. For $m=2.00\,\mathrm{kg}$, $F_{\max}=10.0\,\mathrm N$, $|\mathbf v(0)|=3.00\,\mathrm{m/s}$, $|\mathbf r(0)|=4.00\,\mathrm m$, and $T=5.00\,\mathrm s$, evaluate the bounds. Explain why this does not prevent collision singularities for inverse-square forces.
permittedResults: $|\int_0^t\mathbf a(s)ds|\le\int_0^t|\mathbf a(s)|ds$.
Integrate a uniform acceleration bound twice.
problems.strategy: First: Bound acceleration magnitude by $F_{\max}/m$ and integrate once. Next: Integrate the resulting speed bound to control displacement. Finally: Identify exactly which bounded-force hypothesis fails near a Newtonian point collision.
hints: Bound acceleration magnitude by $F_{\max}/m$ and integrate once.
Integrate the resulting speed bound to control displacement.
Identify exactly which bounded-force hypothesis fails near a Newtonian point collision.
problems.solution:
Since $|\ddot{\mathbf r}|\le F_{\max}/m\equiv a_{\max}$,
$|\mathbf v(t)|\le|\mathbf v_0|+a_{\max}t$ and
$|\mathbf r(t)|\le|\mathbf r_0|+|\mathbf v_0|t+\tfrac12a_{\max}t^2$.
Here $a_{\max}=5.00\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$. For $t<5.00\,\mathrm s$, the bounds are
$|\mathbf v|\le\boxed{28.0\,\mathrm{m/s}}$ and $|\mathbf r|\le4+15+62.5=\boxed{81.5\,\mathrm m}$.
Both are finite, so neither state variable can diverge under the stated hypothesis. For an inverse-square point force, $|\mathbf F|\propto1/r^2$ is unbounded as separation tends to zero; the crucial uniform bound fails, so the argument does not rule out collision singularities.
rubricCriteria: Bounds acceleration magnitude by $F_{\max}/m$ and integrate once.
Integrates the resulting speed bound to control displacement.
Identifies exactly which bounded-force hypothesis fails near a Newtonian point collision.

commonErrors.description: Uses the maximum force directly as an acceleration bound.
commonErrors.consequence: The mass is omitted and the units are wrong.

commonErrors.description: Applies the result to inverse-square collision without checking boundedness.
commonErrors.consequence: It purports to exclude exactly the singularity where the hypothesis fails.

problems.flawedProof: Any deterministic force law prevents finite-time blowup. The bounds are $|v|\le3+10t$ and $|r|\le4+3t+5t^2$, and they apply unchanged to $1/r^2$ gravity.

problems.title: Newtonian similarity rescales time, velocity, and energy together
problems.objective: Newtonian similarity transforms length, time, speed, angular momentum, and both energy terms with consistent exponents.
problems.statement: Let $\mathbf r_i(t)$ solve the Newtonian gravitational $N$-body equations. Prove that $\widetilde{\mathbf r}_i(t)=\lambda\mathbf r_i(t/\lambda^{3/2})$ is another solution for every $\lambda>0$. Derive the scaling of velocity, angular momentum, kinetic energy, potential energy, and orbital period. If a solution has characteristic length $2.00\,\mathrm m$, period $5.00\,\mathrm s$, speed $3.00\,\mathrm{m/s}$, and energy $-12.0\,\mathrm J$, find those quantities for $\lambda=4.00$ with masses unchanged.
permittedResults: Newtonian gravitational acceleration is homogeneous of degree $-2$ in all positions.
Differentiate the rescaled trajectory with the chain rule.
problems.strategy: First: Differentiate the scaled position twice and compare its factor with inverse-square acceleration. Next: Derive velocity and angular-momentum scaling before energy scaling. Finally: Evaluate every requested quantity and check that kinetic and potential energies scale identically.
hints: Differentiate the scaled position twice and compare its factor with inverse-square acceleration.
Derive velocity and angular-momentum scaling before energy scaling.
Evaluate every requested quantity and check that kinetic and potential energies scale identically.
problems.solution:
Two derivatives give $\ddot{\widetilde{\mathbf r}}=\lambda\lambda^{-3}\ddot{\mathbf r}=\lambda^{-2}\ddot{\mathbf r}$, exactly the factor acquired by inverse-square acceleration when all separations scale by $\lambda$. Thus the equations hold. Velocities scale as $\lambda^{-1/2}$, angular momentum as $\lambda^{1/2}$, and both kinetic and gravitational potential energy as $\lambda^{-1}$; periods scale as $\lambda^{3/2}$. For $\lambda=4$:
length $=\boxed{8.00\,\mathrm m}$, period $=5(8)=\boxed{40.0\,\mathrm s}$, speed $=3/2=\boxed{1.50\,\mathrm{m/s}}$, and energy $=-12/4=\boxed{-3.00\,\mathrm J}$. The consistent energy scaling preserves the sign and bound/unbound classification.
rubricCriteria: Differentiates the scaled position twice and compare its factor with inverse-square acceleration.
Derives velocity and angular-momentum scaling before energy scaling.
Evaluates every requested quantity and check that kinetic and potential energies scale identically.

commonErrors.description: Rescales time linearly with length.
commonErrors.consequence: Acceleration and inverse-square force acquire incompatible factors.

commonErrors.description: Rescales kinetic energy but leaves gravitational potential energy unchanged.
commonErrors.consequence: It breaks the similarity of the full energy ledger.

problems.flawedProof: Inverse-square dynamics requires $t\mapsto\lambda t$, so for $\lambda=4$ the period is $20.0\,\mathrm s$ and speed remains $3.00\,\mathrm{m/s}$. Potential energy is unchanged.

problems.title: Uniform gravity is frame-removable but tidal curvature is invariant
problems.objective: Freely falling coordinates remove uniform gravity but preserve the measurable tidal tensor and its vacuum trace signature.
problems.statement: Near a reference worldline expand a gravitational acceleration as $\mathbf g(\mathbf R+\boldsymbol\rho,t)=\mathbf g(\mathbf R,t)+T(t)\boldsymbol\rho+O(\rho^2)$. Construct a translating frame whose origin satisfies $\ddot{\mathbf R}=\mathbf g(\mathbf R,t)$ and derive the leading relative equation for a freely falling test particle. Prove that adding an arbitrary uniform acceleration field to $\mathbf g$ changes the chosen frame motion but not $T=\nabla\mathbf g$. For $T=\operatorname{diag}(2,-1,-1)GM/R^3$, $GM/R^3=4.00\times10^{-7}\,\mathrm{s^{-2}}$, and $\boldsymbol\rho=(10.0,20.0,-30.0)\,\mathrm m$, compute the relative acceleration. Explain the isotropic-trace and point-mass-vacuum checks.
permittedResults: A translating frame subtracts its origin acceleration from every measured acceleration.
The gradient of a spatially uniform vector field is zero.
problems.strategy: First: Subtract the reference-worldline equation from the nearby-particle equation. Next: Differentiate the field after adding a purely time-dependent uniform acceleration. Finally: Apply the tidal tensor numerically and check its trace and units.
hints: Subtract the reference-worldline equation from the nearby-particle equation.
Differentiate the field after adding a purely time-dependent uniform acceleration.
Apply the tidal tensor numerically and check its trace and units.
problems.solution:
Writing $\mathbf r=\mathbf R+\boldsymbol\rho$ gives $\ddot{\boldsymbol\rho}=\mathbf g(\mathbf R+\boldsymbol\rho,t)-\ddot{\mathbf R}$. With the freely falling origin and the expansion,
$\boxed{\ddot{\boldsymbol\rho}=T(t)\boldsymbol\rho+O(\rho^2)}$.
If $\mathbf g\mapsto\mathbf g+\mathbf a_0(t)$, the origin equation gains $\mathbf a_0$, but $\nabla[\mathbf g+\mathbf a_0(t)]=\nabla\mathbf g=T$; relative tidal acceleration is unchanged. Numerically the diagonal entries are $(8,-4,-4)\times10^{-7}\,\mathrm{s^{-2}}$, so
$\ddot{\boldsymbol\rho}=\boxed{(8.00,-8.00,12.0)\times10^{-6}\,\mathrm{m/s^2}}$.
The tensor trace is zero, $2-1-1=0$, consistent with a vacuum point-mass field away from the source. An isotropic tensor would have nonzero trace unless it vanished, signaling local source density rather than removable uniform gravity.
rubricCriteria: Subtracts the reference-worldline equation from the nearby-particle equation.
Differentiates the field after adding a purely time-dependent uniform acceleration.
Applies the tidal tensor numerically and check its trace and units.

commonErrors.description: Retains the uniform reference acceleration in the relative equation.
commonErrors.consequence: A removable common fall is misidentified as a tidal observable.

commonErrors.description: Treats the point-mass tidal tensor as isotropic.
commonErrors.consequence: It loses radial stretching, transverse compression, and the vacuum zero trace.

problems.flawedProof: The relative acceleration is $\mathbf g(\mathbf R,t)+T\boldsymbol\rho$, so adding a uniform field changes local tides. A point mass produces an isotropic tensor proportional to the identity.

problems.title: Polar Euler-Lagrange equations recover straight inertial motion
problems.objective: Polar kinetic geometry recovers free Cartesian motion, conserved angular momentum, and the outward coordinate acceleration.
problems.statement: A free particle of mass $m$ moves in a plane with polar coordinates $(r,\theta)$ and Lagrangian $L=m(\dot r^2+r^2\dot\theta^2)/2$. Derive both Euler-Lagrange equations and identify the conserved generalized momentum. For $m=2.00\,\mathrm{kg}$, $r=3.00\,\mathrm m$, $\dot r=1.00\,\mathrm{m/s}$, and $\dot\theta=0.500\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$, compute the instantaneous radial acceleration and angular momentum. Check the purely radial limit.
permittedResults: Euler-Lagrange is $d(\partial L/\partial\dot q)/dt-\partial L/\partial q=0$.
problems.strategy: First: Apply Euler-Lagrange separately to the radial and angular coordinates. Next: Use the absence of the angle itself to identify a cyclic momentum. Finally: Insert the signed rates and check radial-acceleration and angular-momentum units.
hints: Apply Euler-Lagrange separately to the radial and angular coordinates.
Use the absence of the angle itself to identify a cyclic momentum.
Insert the signed rates and check radial-acceleration and angular-momentum units.
problems.solution: For $r$, $d(m\dot r)/dt-mr\dot\theta^2=0$, so $\boxed{\ddot r=r\dot\theta^2}$. For $\theta$, $d(mr^2\dot\theta)/dt=0$, so $\boxed{p_\theta=mr^2\dot\theta}$ is conserved. Numerically, $\ddot r=3(0.5)^2=\boxed{0.750\,\mathrm{m/s^2}}$ and $p_\theta=2(3)^2(0.5)=\boxed{9.00\,\mathrm{kg\,m^2/s}}$. The positive coordinate acceleration is the polar-coordinate term needed for zero Cartesian acceleration; it is not an outward force. If $\dot\theta\to0$, radial acceleration vanishes and $r$ changes linearly.
rubricCriteria: Applies Euler-Lagrange separately to the radial and angular coordinates.
Uses the absence of the angle itself to identify a cyclic momentum.
Inserts the signed rates and check radial-acceleration and angular-momentum units.

commonErrors.description: Adds a minus sign to the radial coordinate acceleration.
commonErrors.consequence: It confuses the polar-coordinate equation with a centripetal force law.

commonErrors.description: Calls angular velocity rather than angular momentum the cyclic constant.
commonErrors.consequence: It ignores changes in radius along a free straight-line trajectory.

problems.flawedProof: Euler-Lagrange gives $\ddot r=-r\dot\theta^2$, and cyclicity makes $\dot\theta$ constant. Thus the free particle experiences a physical inward force.

problems.title: A nonlinear coordinate preserves the free-particle equation
problems.objective: Nonlinear coordinate transformation reproduces the free-particle equation and distinguishes coordinate acceleration from force.
problems.statement: On the half-line $x>0$, introduce $q>0$ by $x=q^2$. Starting from $L=m\dot x^2/2$, express the Lagrangian in $q$, derive its Euler-Lagrange equation, and show it is exactly equivalent to $\ddot x=0$. If $q(0)=2.00\,\mathrm{m^{1/2}}$ and $\dot q(0)=0.500\,\mathrm{m^{1/2}/s}$, compute $\ddot q(0)$ and $\dot x(0)$. Explain why the apparent nonlinear term is coordinate geometry rather than a force.
permittedResults: $\dot x=2q\dot q$ and $\ddot x=2(\dot q^2+q\ddot q)$.
problems.strategy: First: Substitute the coordinate derivative into the Cartesian kinetic Lagrangian. Next: Differentiate both the coordinate-dependent momentum and the Lagrangian with respect to $q$. Finally: Compare the resulting equation with the chain-rule expression for $\ddot x$ and audit units.
hints: Substitute the coordinate derivative into the Cartesian kinetic Lagrangian.
Differentiate both the coordinate-dependent momentum and the Lagrangian with respect to $q$.
Compare the resulting equation with the chain-rule expression for $\ddot x$ and audit units.
problems.solution:
Substitution gives $L=2mq^2\dot q^2$. Then $\partial L/\partial\dot q=4mq^2\dot q$ and $\partial L/\partial q=4mq\dot q^2$. Euler-Lagrange yields
$4mq^2\ddot q+4mq\dot q^2=0$, or $\boxed{q\ddot q+\dot q^2=0}$. But $\ddot x=2(q\ddot q+\dot q^2)$, so this is precisely free motion. Initially $\ddot q=-\dot q^2/q=-0.25/2=\boxed{-0.125\,\mathrm{m^{1/2}/s^2}}$ and $\dot x=2q\dot q=\boxed{2.00\,\mathrm{m/s}}$. The nonlinear coordinate acceleration compensates the nonlinear map; no physical force is present.
rubricCriteria: Substitutes the coordinate derivative into the Cartesian kinetic Lagrangian.
Differentiates both the coordinate-dependent momentum and the Lagrangian with respect to $q$.
Compares the resulting equation with the chain-rule expression for $\ddot x$ and audit units.

commonErrors.description: Treats the transformed kinetic coefficient as a constant.
commonErrors.consequence: Coordinate-metric variation is omitted, so the transformed equation no longer represents free Cartesian motion.

commonErrors.description: Interprets nonzero coordinate acceleration as a physical force.
commonErrors.consequence: It assigns dynamics to a change of variables.

problems.flawedProof: The transformed Lagrangian is $2m\dot q^2$, so $\ddot q=0$ and $\ddot x=2\dot q^2\ne0$. The coordinate change creates a real force.

problems.title: Rayleigh dissipation supplies the correct damping sign
problems.objective: Rayleigh differentiation supplies the damping sign, instantaneous acceleration, and strictly nonpositive mechanical power.
problems.statement: A generalized coordinate has $L=m\dot q^2/2-kq^2/2$ and Rayleigh function $\mathcal R=c\dot q^2/2$. Use the dissipative Euler-Lagrange equation to derive the motion and the mechanical-energy rate. For $m=2.00\,\mathrm{kg}$, $k=18.0\,\mathrm{N/m}$, $c=4.00\,\mathrm{kg/s}$, $q=0.300\,\mathrm m$, and $\dot q=-0.500\,\mathrm{m/s}$, compute $\ddot q$ and $\dot E$. Check the $c\to0$ limit.
permittedResults: With Rayleigh dissipation, $dL_{\dot q}/dt-L_q=-\partial\mathcal R/\partial\dot q$.
problems.strategy: First: Differentiate the Rayleigh function with respect to generalized velocity. Next: Multiply the resulting equation by velocity to derive the energy rate. Finally: Insert the signed displacement and velocity and verify that dissipation power is never positive.
hints: Differentiate the Rayleigh function with respect to generalized velocity.
Multiply the resulting equation by velocity to derive the energy rate.
Insert the signed displacement and velocity and verify that dissipation power is never positive.
problems.solution:
The equation is $m\ddot q+kq=-c\dot q$, or $m\ddot q+c\dot q+kq=0$. Thus
$\ddot q=-(c\dot q+kq)/m=-[4(-0.5)+18(0.3)]/2=\boxed{-1.70\,\mathrm{m/s^2}}$.
For $E=m\dot q^2/2+kq^2/2$, multiplication by $\dot q$ gives
$\dot E=-c\dot q^2=\boxed{-1.00\,\mathrm W}$. The sign is negative independent of the velocity direction. As $c\to0$, the Rayleigh force and energy loss vanish, leaving the conservative oscillator.
rubricCriteria: Differentiates the Rayleigh function with respect to generalized velocity.
Multiplies the resulting equation by velocity to derive the energy rate.
Inserts the signed displacement and velocity and verify that dissipation power is never positive.

commonErrors.description: Uses the positive velocity derivative of the Rayleigh function as the generalized force.
commonErrors.consequence: Damping injects rather than removes energy.

commonErrors.description: Uses signed velocity rather than velocity squared for dissipated power.
commonErrors.consequence: Signed-velocity dissipation predicts energy gain for motion in the negative coordinate direction.

problems.flawedProof: The Rayleigh force is $+c\dot q$, so $m\ddot q-c\dot q+kq=0$ and $\dot E=-c\dot q=+2.00\,\mathrm W$.

problems.title: A time-dependent scale coordinate generates inertial cross terms
problems.objective: Time-dependent scaling generates the complete inertial cross terms required for equivalence with free motion.
problems.statement: A free particle on a line is described by $x=a(t)q$, where $a(t)>0$ is prescribed. Derive the transformed Lagrangian and Euler-Lagrange equation for $q$. Show directly that it is equivalent to $\ddot x=0$. For $a(t)=1+t/T$, $T=2.00\,\mathrm s$, and at $t=2.00\,\mathrm s$ take $q=3.00\,\mathrm m$ and $\dot q=-0.500\,\mathrm{m/s}$. Compute $\ddot q$ and check dimensions.
permittedResults: $\dot x=a\dot q+\dot a q$.
$\ddot x=a\ddot q+2\dot a\dot q+\ddot a q$.
problems.strategy: First: Retain the full squared velocity including its cross term. Next: Apply Euler-Lagrange with the prescribed time functions held fixed in partial derivatives. Finally: Compare with the chain-rule acceleration and insert the linear scale factor.
hints: Retain the full squared velocity including its cross term.
Apply Euler-Lagrange with the prescribed time functions held fixed in partial derivatives.
Compare with the chain-rule acceleration and insert the linear scale factor.
problems.solution:
The transformed Lagrangian is
$L=\tfrac12m(a\dot q+\dot aq)^2$. Euler-Lagrange simplification gives
$\boxed{a\ddot q+2\dot a\dot q+\ddot aq=0}$,
which is exactly $\ddot x=0$. At $t=2\,\mathrm s$, $a=2$, $\dot a=1/T=0.500\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$, and $\ddot a=0$. Hence
$\ddot q=-2\dot a\dot q/a=-2(0.5)(-0.5)/2=\boxed{0.250\,\mathrm{m/s^2}}$.
The nonzero coordinate acceleration compensates the expanding coordinate scale. If $a$ becomes constant, both inertial terms vanish and $\ddot q=0$.
rubricCriteria: Retains the full squared velocity including its cross term.
Applies Euler-Lagrange with the prescribed time functions held fixed in partial derivatives.
Compares with the chain-rule acceleration and insert the linear scale factor.

commonErrors.description: Drops the velocity cross term from the transformed kinetic energy.
commonErrors.consequence: The resulting equation misses the factor-two scale-rate term.

commonErrors.description: Treats the prescribed scale factor as a dynamical coordinate.
commonErrors.consequence: It introduces an extra Euler-Lagrange equation not present in the model.

problems.flawedProof: The Lagrangian is $ma^2\dot q^2/2$, so $a^2\ddot q+a\dot a\dot q=0$ and $\ddot q=0.125\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$.

problems.title: Arc-length metric turns a smooth track into one generalized coordinate
problems.objective: Track-induced kinetic metric determines the exact tangential equation, curvature term, and horizontal-track limit.
problems.statement: A bead moves without friction on the fixed planar track $x=q$, $y=\beta q^2$ in uniform gravity. Derive the reduced Lagrangian and the exact equation for $q$. For $\beta=0.500\,\mathrm{m^{-1}}$, $q=1.00\,\mathrm m$, $\dot q=2.00\,\mathrm{m/s}$, and $g=9.81\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$, compute $\ddot q$. Identify the geometric term and check the $\beta\to0$ limit.
permittedResults: The bead speed is $v^2=\dot x^2+\dot y^2$.
Gravitational potential is $mgy$.
problems.strategy: First: Compute the induced metric factor from the track derivatives. Next: Apply Euler-Lagrange before substituting numerical values. Finally: Separate the velocity-dependent curvature term from gravity and test the flat-track limit.
hints: Compute the induced metric factor from the track derivatives.
Apply Euler-Lagrange before substituting numerical values.
Separate the velocity-dependent curvature term from gravity and test the flat-track limit.
problems.solution:
Since $\dot x=\dot q$ and $\dot y=2\beta q\dot q$,
$L=\tfrac12m(1+4\beta^2q^2)\dot q^2-mg\beta q^2$. Euler-Lagrange gives
$(1+4\beta^2q^2)\ddot q+4\beta^2q\dot q^2+2g\beta q=0$.
For the data, the metric factor is $2$, the geometric term is $4(0.25)(1)(4)=4.00\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$, and gravity term is $2(9.81)(0.5)(1)=9.81\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$. Therefore
$\boxed{\ddot q=-(4.00+9.81)/2=-6.905\,\mathrm{m/s^2}}$. As $\beta\to0$, the track becomes horizontal and every extra term vanishes, yielding uniform motion.
rubricCriteria: Computes the induced metric factor from the track derivatives.
Applies Euler-Lagrange before substituting numerical values.
Separates the velocity-dependent curvature term from gravity and test the flat-track limit.

commonErrors.description: Uses the Cartesian horizontal speed as the full bead speed.
commonErrors.consequence: Induced track metric and curvature acceleration are both absent from the claimed dynamics.

commonErrors.description: Drops the velocity-dependent term when differentiating the metric coefficient.
commonErrors.consequence: The equation fails at nonzero track speed.

problems.flawedProof: The reduced Lagrangian is $m\dot q^2/2-mg\beta q^2$, so $\ddot q=-2g\beta q=-9.81\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$. Track curvature does not affect tangential dynamics.

problems.title: Cyclic reduction of a pendulum on a freely translating support
problems.objective: Cyclic reduction of a pendulum on a freely translating support eliminates the support coordinate and predicts coupled acceleration and small-angle frequency.
problems.statement:
A cart of mass $M$ moves without friction along a horizontal inertial axis. A pendulum bob of mass $m$ is attached to the cart by a massless rod of length $\ell$. Let $X$ be the cart position and let $\theta$ be the rod angle measured from the downward vertical. There is no horizontal external force.

Derive the two-coordinate Lagrangian and identify the cyclic momentum $P$. For the sector $P=0$, eliminate $\dot X$ by a Routh reduction and obtain the one-coordinate reduced Routhian. Derive the exact equation for $\theta$ and its small-angle frequency about the downward equilibrium.

For $M=3.00\,\mathrm{kg}$, $m=1.00\,\mathrm{kg}$, $\ell=0.800\,\mathrm m$, $g=9.81\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$, $\theta=20.0^\circ$, and $\dot\theta=0$ in the $P=0$ sector, compute $\ddot\theta$ and the simultaneous cart acceleration $\ddot X$. Compute the small-angle frequency. Check the limits $M\to\infty$ and $m\to0$ without dividing by the bob mass before forming the reduced dynamics.
permittedResults: A cyclic coordinate has conserved canonical momentum, and its fixed-momentum Routhian is obtained by subtracting $P\dot X$ before eliminating $\dot X$.
For a reduced Lagrangian $R=\tfrac12A(\theta)\dot\theta^2-V(\theta)$, Euler--Lagrange gives $A\ddot\theta+\tfrac12A'\dot\theta^2+V'=0$.
problems.strategy: Construct the bob velocity from its moving pivot, isolate the conserved horizontal momentum, and eliminate the support speed at fixed $P=0$. Differentiate the momentum relation once more to recover the cart acceleration after solving the reduced angular equation.
hints: Use $x_b=X+\ell\sin\theta$ and $y_b=-\ell\cos\theta$ before expanding the kinetic energy.
At $P=0$, solve $\dot X=-m\ell\cos\theta\,\dot\theta/(M+m)$ and substitute into $L-P\dot X$.
When $\dot\theta=0$, differentiate the zero-momentum relation to obtain $\ddot X=-m\ell\cos\theta\,\ddot\theta/(M+m)$.
problems.solution:
The bob velocity components are
$\dot x_b=\dot X+\ell\cos\theta\,\dot\theta$ and
$\dot y_b=\ell\sin\theta\,\dot\theta$. Thus
$$
L=\frac12(M+m)\dot X^2+m\ell\cos\theta\,\dot X\dot\theta
+\frac12m\ell^2\dot\theta^2+mg\ell\cos\theta.
$$
Horizontal translation is cyclic, with
$$
\boxed{P=(M+m)\dot X+m\ell\cos\theta\,\dot\theta}.
$$
For $P=0$,
$$
\dot X=-\frac{m\ell\cos\theta}{M+m}\dot\theta.
$$
The fixed-momentum Routhian $R=L-P\dot X$ therefore becomes
$$
\boxed{R_0=\frac12m\ell^2\left(1-\frac{m}{M+m}\cos^2\theta\right)\dot\theta^2
+mg\ell\cos\theta}.
$$
Writing $\mu=m/(M+m)$, Euler--Lagrange gives
$$
\boxed{\ell(1-\mu\cos^2\theta)\ddot\theta
+\ell\mu\sin\theta\cos\theta\,\dot\theta^2+g\sin\theta=0}.
$$
Linearization at $\theta=0$ yields
$$
\ddot\theta+\omega_0^2\theta=0,
\qquad
\boxed{\omega_0^2=\frac{g(M+m)}{\ell M}}.
$$

At the stated instant, $\mu=1/4$ and $\dot\theta=0$, so
$$
\ddot\theta=-\frac{g\sin20^\circ}{\ell[1-(1/4)\cos^2 20^\circ]}
=\boxed{-5.38\,\mathrm{s^{-2}}}.
$$
Differentiating $P=0$ at zero angular speed gives
$$
\ddot X=-\frac{m\ell\cos\theta}{M+m}\ddot\theta
=\boxed{1.01\,\mathrm{m/s^2}}.
$$
Finally,
$$
\omega_0=\sqrt{\frac{(9.81)(4.00)}{(0.800)(3.00)}}
=\boxed{4.04\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}}.
$$
As $M\to\infty$, support recoil vanishes and $\omega_0\to\sqrt{g/\ell}$. As $m\to0$ with a nonzero test bob retained through the equations, the same fixed-pivot limit emerges; the common factor $m$ cancels only after the reduced variational equation has been formed.
rubricCriteria: Constructs the moving-pivot kinetic cross term and identifies the conserved total horizontal momentum $P$.
Performs fixed-$P$ Routh reduction and derives the angle-dependent reduced mass and exact angular equation.
Computes $\ddot\theta=-5.38\,\mathrm{s^{-2}}$, $\ddot X=1.01\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$, and $\omega_0=4.04\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$ with correct limits.

commonErrors.description: Substitutes the support velocity into $L$ without imposing the fixed cyclic momentum or forming the Routhian.
commonErrors.consequence: The reduced kinetic coefficient acquires the wrong sign and no longer reproduces horizontal-momentum conservation.

commonErrors.description: Treats the cart as fixed when deriving the small-angle equation.
commonErrors.consequence: Support recoil is suppressed and the predicted frequency is too low for finite $M$.

problems.flawedProof: Because $X$ is cyclic it may be set to a constant. The reduced Lagrangian is therefore that of a fixed pendulum, $m\ell^2\dot\theta^2/2+mg\ell\cos\theta$, and $\omega_0=\sqrt{g/\ell}=3.50\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$ with $\ddot X=0$.

problems.title: A translating coordinate makes canonical and mechanical momentum differ
problems.objective: Translating coordinates distinguish canonical from frame-relative mechanical momentum and recover the compensating coordinate acceleration.
problems.statement: A free particle has inertial position $x=q+X(t)$ with prescribed $X(t)$. Derive the Lagrangian in $q$, its canonical momentum, and the Euler-Lagrange equation. For $m=3.00\,\mathrm{kg}$, $\dot q=-2.00\,\mathrm{m/s}$, and $\dot X=5.00\,\mathrm{m/s}$, compute canonical momentum and compare it with $m\dot q$. If $\ddot X=1.50\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$, find $\ddot q$. Explain which momentum is conserved when $X$ has constant velocity.
permittedResults: $\dot x=\dot q+\dot X$.
problems.strategy: First: Substitute the full inertial velocity before differentiating with respect to generalized velocity. Next: Use cyclicity of $q$ to identify the conserved canonical momentum. Finally: Distinguish inertial mechanical momentum from mass times coordinate velocity and test constant frame velocity.
hints: Substitute the full inertial velocity before differentiating with respect to generalized velocity.
Use cyclicity of $q$ to identify the conserved canonical momentum.
Distinguish inertial mechanical momentum from mass times coordinate velocity and test constant frame velocity.
problems.solution:
The Lagrangian is $L=m(\dot q+\dot X)^2/2$. Thus
$p_q=\partial L/\partial\dot q=m(\dot q+\dot X)=m\dot x$ and, since $q$ is cyclic, $\dot p_q=0$. This gives $\ddot q=-\ddot X$. Numerically,
$p_q=3(-2+5)=\boxed{9.00\,\mathrm{kg\,m/s}}$, whereas $m\dot q=-6.00\,\mathrm{kg\,m/s}$. With $\ddot X=1.50$, $\boxed{\ddot q=-1.50\,\mathrm{m/s^2}}$. If $\dot X$ is constant, both $p_q=m\dot x$ and $m\dot q=p_q-m\dot X$ are constant, but they are different frame-dependent values.
rubricCriteria: Substitutes the full inertial velocity before differentiating with respect to generalized velocity.
Uses cyclicity of $q$ to identify the conserved canonical momentum.
Distinguishes inertial mechanical momentum from mass times coordinate velocity and test constant frame velocity.

commonErrors.description: Defines canonical momentum as mass times generalized-coordinate velocity only.
commonErrors.consequence: Prescribed frame velocity disappears from canonical momentum despite its presence in the kinetic energy.

commonErrors.description: Sets generalized-coordinate acceleration to the frame acceleration.
commonErrors.consequence: The inertial compensation sign is reversed.

problems.flawedProof: The canonical momentum is $m\dot q=-6.00\,\mathrm{kg\,m/s}$. Since it is conserved, $\ddot q=0$ even when the coordinate frame accelerates.

problems.title: Generalized force dimensions follow the coordinate dimension
problems.objective: Virtual work converts a Cartesian force into the dimensionally correct angular generalized force on an ellipse.
