problems.statement: A force $\mathbf F=(F_x,F_y)$ acts on a particle constrained by $x=a\cos\theta$, $y=b\sin\theta$. Derive the generalized force $Q_\theta$ from virtual work. For $a=2.00\,\mathrm m$, $b=1.00\,\mathrm m$, $\theta=\pi/6$, and $\mathbf F=(3.00,4.00)\,\mathrm N$, compute $Q_\theta$. Explain why its units are torque rather than force and verify the circular limit $a=b$.
permittedResults: Virtual work is $\delta W=\mathbf F\cdot\delta\mathbf r=Q_\theta\delta\theta$.
problems.strategy: First: Differentiate the constrained position with respect to the angular coordinate. Next: Take the force dot product with that tangent vector. Finally: Evaluate the signed result and interpret radians as dimensionless.
hints: Differentiate the constrained position with respect to the angular coordinate.
Take the force dot product with that tangent vector.
Evaluate the signed result and interpret radians as dimensionless.
problems.solution:
Since $\partial\mathbf r/\partial\theta=(-a\sin\theta,b\cos\theta)$,
$Q_\theta=\mathbf F\cdot\partial\mathbf r/\partial\theta=-aF_x\sin\theta+bF_y\cos\theta$.
For the data,
$Q_\theta=-2(3)(1/2)+1(4)(\sqrt3/2)=-3+2\sqrt3=\boxed{0.464\,\mathrm{N\,m}}$.
Because $\delta\theta$ is dimensionless, $Q_\theta$ must have energy/torque units so that $Q_\theta\delta\theta$ is work. If $a=b=R$, the result becomes $R\mathbf F\cdot\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}$, the usual torque component about the center.
rubricCriteria: Differentiates the constrained position with respect to the angular coordinate.
Takes the force dot product with that tangent vector.
Evaluates the signed result and interpret radians as dimensionless.

commonErrors.description: Uses the radial rather than tangent derivative of the constrained position.
commonErrors.consequence: The generalized force does not reproduce virtual work.

commonErrors.description: Reports the generalized angular force in newtons.
commonErrors.consequence: The virtual-work equation is dimensionally inconsistent.

problems.flawedProof: The generalized force is the force magnitude $5.00\,\mathrm N$ because the coordinate is dimensionless. No lever-arm factor is required.

problems.title: A cylinder geodesic unwraps to a straight line
problems.objective: Cylinder cyclicity unwraps the geodesic into a straight line and determines helix pitch with its axial boundary case.
problems.statement: A free bead is constrained to a cylinder of radius $R$ with coordinates $(\phi,z)$ and $L=m(R^2\dot\phi^2+\dot z^2)/2$. Derive both constants of motion and the path equation $z(\phi)$. For $R=0.500\,\mathrm m$, $\dot\phi=4.00\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$, $\dot z=1.50\,\mathrm{m/s}$, and initial $(\phi,z)=(0,0)$, find $z$ after two full turns and the helix pitch per turn. Verify the $\dot\phi\to0$ boundary.
permittedResults: Both coordinates are cyclic in the free constrained Lagrangian.
One full turn changes $\phi$ by $2\pi$.
problems.strategy: First: Identify the two canonical momenta before solving the motion. Next: Eliminate time using the constant ratio $dz/d\phi$. Finally: Evaluate the two-turn displacement and distinguish a zero angular rate from an infinite slope artifact.
hints: Identify the two canonical momenta before solving the motion.
Eliminate time using the constant ratio $dz/d\phi$.
Evaluate the two-turn displacement and distinguish a zero angular rate from an infinite slope artifact.
problems.solution:
Cyclicity gives $p_\phi=mR^2\dot\phi$ and $p_z=m\dot z$, both constant, so $\phi=\phi_0+\dot\phi t$ and $z=z_0+\dot zt$. Eliminating time,
$\boxed{z-z_0=(\dot z/\dot\phi)(\phi-\phi_0)}$.
The pitch per turn is $2\pi\dot z/\dot\phi=2\pi(1.5/4)=\boxed{2.356\,\mathrm m}$. After two turns, $z=\boxed{4.712\,\mathrm m}$. Unwrapping the cylinder with coordinate $s=R\phi$ makes this a straight line. If $\dot\phi\to0$ with nonzero $\dot z$, the bead follows a generator at fixed angle; $z(\phi)$ is then not a useful graph, though the trajectory is regular.
rubricCriteria: Identifies the two canonical momenta before solving the motion.
Eliminates time using the constant ratio $dz/d\phi$.
Evaluates the two-turn displacement and distinguish a zero angular rate from an infinite slope artifact.

commonErrors.description: Treats angular velocity as inversely proportional to radius during fixed-radius motion.
commonErrors.consequence: It invents a radial equation absent from the constraint.

commonErrors.description: Uses one radian rather than one full turn to compute pitch.
commonErrors.consequence: The axial displacement is too small by a factor of two pi.

problems.flawedProof: The cylinder curvature causes $\ddot\phi=-\dot z^2/R^2$, so the path is not a helix. The pitch is simply $\dot z/\dot\phi=0.375\,\mathrm m$.

problems.title: An expanding circular constraint performs calculable work
problems.objective: A prescribed expanding constraint transfers calculable power while conserving angular momentum rather than angular speed.
problems.statement: A bead moves freely on a horizontal circular hoop whose prescribed radius is $a(t)$. With angular coordinate $\theta$, derive the reduced Lagrangian, conserved angular momentum, and exact mechanical-energy rate. For $m=1.50\,\mathrm{kg}$, $a=2.00\,\mathrm m$, $\dot a=0.200\,\mathrm{m/s}$, $\ddot a=0$, and conserved $p_\theta=6.00\,\mathrm{kg\,m^2/s}$, compute $\dot\theta$, kinetic energy, and its instantaneous rate. Check the fixed-radius limit.
permittedResults: The bead speed is $v^2=\dot a^2+a^2\dot\theta^2$ when the hoop expands radially.
A cyclic coordinate has conserved canonical momentum even when the Lagrangian depends explicitly on time.
problems.strategy: First: Include both radial motion imposed by the hoop and tangential bead motion in kinetic energy. Next: Use angular cyclicity to express angular rate in terms of the conserved momentum. Finally: Differentiate kinetic energy along the equations, retaining prescribed radial acceleration unless a local value is specified.
hints: Include both radial motion imposed by the hoop and tangential bead motion in kinetic energy.
Use angular cyclicity to express angular rate in terms of the conserved momentum.
Differentiate kinetic energy along the equations, retaining prescribed radial acceleration unless a local value is specified.
problems.solution:
The reduced Lagrangian is $L=\tfrac12m(\dot a^2+a^2\dot\theta^2)$ and $p_\theta=ma^2\dot\theta$ is conserved. Thus $\dot\theta=6/[1.5(4)]=\boxed{1.00\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}}$ and
$K=\tfrac12(1.5)[0.2^2+4(1)^2]=\boxed{3.03\,\mathrm J}$. In general,
$\dot K=m\dot a\ddot a+ma\dot a\dot\theta^2+ma^2\dot\theta\ddot\theta$.
Conservation of $ma^2\dot\theta$ gives $a\ddot\theta=-2\dot a\dot\theta$, so
$\boxed{\dot K=m\dot a(\ddot a-a\dot\theta^2)}$. If the stated instant lies in constant-rate expansion, $\ddot a=0$, then $\dot K=1.5(0.2)(-2)(1)^2=\boxed{-0.600\,\mathrm W}$: the hoop removes tangential energy while enforcing outward motion. For fixed radius, $\dot a=0$ and the power vanishes.
rubricCriteria: Includes both radial motion imposed by the hoop and tangential bead motion in kinetic energy.
Uses angular cyclicity to express angular rate in terms of the conserved momentum.
Differentiates kinetic energy along the equations, retaining prescribed radial acceleration unless a local value is specified.

commonErrors.description: Omits the imposed radial speed from kinetic energy.
commonErrors.consequence: It loses part of the constraint work and understates total energy.

commonErrors.description: Assumes angular speed is conserved because angle is cyclic.
commonErrors.consequence: It ignores conservation of angular momentum as radius changes.

problems.flawedProof: Cyclicity makes $\dot\theta$ constant, so expansion increases $K$ at rate $ma\dot a\dot\theta^2=+0.600\,\mathrm W$. The radial kinetic term is not part of bead energy.

problems.title: Spherical-pendulum reduction exposes a centrifugal barrier
problems.objective: Spherical-pendulum reduction produces the azimuthal centrifugal barrier and its polar accessibility condition.
problems.statement: A mass $m$ is constrained to a sphere of radius $\ell$ in gravity with polar angle $\theta$ measured from downward vertical and azimuth $\phi$. Derive the Lagrangian, conserved $p_\phi$, and a one-coordinate energy equation for $\theta$. For $m=1.00\,\mathrm{kg}$, $\ell=2.00\,\mathrm m$, $p_\phi=3.00\,\mathrm{kg\,m^2/s}$, and $\theta=\pi/3$, compute the effective centrifugal term in the potential and show its behavior as $\theta\to0$.
permittedResults: On a sphere, $v^2=\ell^2(\dot\theta^2+\sin^2\theta\dot\phi^2)$.
With downward-zero convention, $U=mg\ell(1-\cos\theta)$.
problems.strategy: First: Write kinetic energy using the spherical metric and identify azimuthal cyclicity. Next: Eliminate angular velocity using $p_\phi$ before writing the energy. Finally: Evaluate the inverse-sine-squared barrier and inspect the polar limit.
hints: Write kinetic energy using the spherical metric and identify azimuthal cyclicity.
Eliminate angular velocity using $p_\phi$ before writing the energy.
Evaluate the inverse-sine-squared barrier and inspect the polar limit.
problems.solution:
The Lagrangian is
$L=\tfrac12m\ell^2(\dot\theta^2+\sin^2\theta\dot\phi^2)-mg\ell(1-\cos\theta)$.
Cyclicity gives $p_\phi=m\ell^2\sin^2\theta\dot\phi$. Energy becomes
$E=\tfrac12m\ell^2\dot\theta^2+U_{\rm eff}(\theta)$ with
$\boxed{U_{\rm eff}=mg\ell(1-\cos\theta)+\frac{p_\phi^2}{2m\ell^2\sin^2\theta}}$.
At $\theta=\pi/3$, the centrifugal contribution is $9/[2(1)(4)(3/4)]=\boxed{1.50\,\mathrm J}$. For nonzero $p_\phi$, it diverges like $p_\phi^2/(2m\ell^2\theta^2)$ as $\theta\to0$, preventing the trajectory from reaching the axis. If $p_\phi=0$, that barrier disappears.
rubricCriteria: Writes kinetic energy using the spherical metric and identify azimuthal cyclicity.
Eliminates angular velocity using $p_\phi$ before writing the energy.
Evaluates the inverse-sine-squared barrier and inspect the polar limit.

commonErrors.description: Eliminates azimuthal velocity without squaring the sine factor correctly.
commonErrors.consequence: Azimuthal elimination gives the barrier the wrong sine dependence.

commonErrors.description: Claims the centrifugal term vanishes at the polar axis.
commonErrors.consequence: Polar accessibility is reversed by making the nonzero-momentum barrier vanish at the axis.

problems.flawedProof: Substituting $p_\phi$ gives a centrifugal potential $p_\phi^2\sin^2\theta/(2m\ell^2)$, which vanishes at the pole.

problems.title: Cycloidal arc length converts gravity into an exact harmonic oscillator
problems.objective: Cycloidal arc length turns gravity into an exact harmonic potential and proves amplitude-independent period.
problems.statement: For an inverted cycloidal track, let signed arc length $s$ from the lowest point satisfy the geometric identity $y=s^2/(8a)$, where $y$ is height and $a>0$. Use $s$ as the generalized coordinate to derive the exact equation and oscillation period for a frictionless bead. For $a=0.500\,\mathrm m$ and $g=9.81\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$, compute the period. Explain why it is independent of release amplitude within the ideal cycloidal model and compare the $a\to\infty$ limit.
permittedResults: Arc length makes the kinetic energy $m\dot s^2/2$.
A harmonic oscillator $\ddot s+\omega^2s=0$ has period $2\pi/\omega$.
problems.strategy: First: Insert the exact height-arc relation into gravitational potential energy. Next: Apply Euler-Lagrange directly in signed arc length. Finally: Compute the period and identify why no higher powers of $s$ produce amplitude dependence.
hints: Insert the exact height-arc relation into gravitational potential energy.
Apply Euler-Lagrange directly in signed arc length.
Compute the period and identify why no higher powers of $s$ produce amplitude dependence.
problems.solution:
The reduced Lagrangian is $L=m\dot s^2/2-mg s^2/(8a)$. Euler-Lagrange gives
$m\ddot s+mg s/(4a)=0$, so $\boxed{\omega=\sqrt{g/(4a)}}$ and
$\boxed{P=4\pi\sqrt{a/g}}$. For $a=0.500\,\mathrm m$, $P=4\pi\sqrt{0.5/9.81}=\boxed{2.837\,\mathrm s}$. Because the exact potential is quadratic in arc length, every allowed amplitude has the same period, not merely small amplitudes. As $a\to\infty$, curvature and restoring coefficient vanish and the period diverges toward free motion.
rubricCriteria: Inserts the exact height-arc relation into gravitational potential energy.
Applies Euler-Lagrange directly in signed arc length.
Computes the period and identify why no higher powers of $s$ produce amplitude dependence.

commonErrors.description: Uses vertical height itself as arc length.
commonErrors.consequence: Arc-height confusion turns the quadratic cycloidal potential into a linear one.

commonErrors.description: Treats the result as a small-angle approximation.
commonErrors.consequence: Exact cycloidal isochrony is demoted incorrectly to a small-amplitude approximation.

problems.flawedProof: Since $y=s$, the equation is $\ddot s=-g$ and the return time depends on release height. A cycloid is only approximately isochronous.

problems.title: Vertical support acceleration renormalizes pendulum gravity
problems.objective: Vertically accelerated support motion renormalizes pendulum gravity with the correct free-fall and static limits.
problems.statement: A pendulum of length $\ell$ has a support with prescribed upward coordinate $Y(t)$ in an inertial frame. Take $x=\ell\sin\theta$ and $y=Y-\ell\cos\theta$. Derive the Lagrangian up to terms independent of $\theta$ and obtain the exact equation. If $\ddot Y=+3.00\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$, $\ell=1.20\,\mathrm m$, and $\theta=20.0^\circ$ with $\dot\theta=0$, compute $\ddot\theta$. State the free-fall-support and static-support limits.
permittedResults: The inertial kinetic energy uses both $\dot x$ and $\dot y$.
Terms depending on time alone do not affect the Euler-Lagrange equation for $\theta$.
problems.strategy: First: Expand the support-bead velocity and retain the cross term involving support speed. Next: Apply Euler-Lagrange before replacing support acceleration by its value. Finally: Interpret the combination of gravity and upward support acceleration and test free fall.
hints: Expand the support-bead velocity and retain the cross term involving support speed.
Apply Euler-Lagrange before replacing support acceleration by its value.
Interpret the combination of gravity and upward support acceleration and test free fall.
problems.solution:
After dropping $m\dot Y^2/2-mgY$, the relevant Lagrangian is
$L=\tfrac12m\ell^2\dot\theta^2+m\ell\dot Y\sin\theta\dot\theta+mg\ell\cos\theta$.
Euler-Lagrange cancellation of the $\dot Y\cos\theta\dot\theta$ terms leaves
$\boxed{\ell\ddot\theta+(g+\ddot Y)\sin\theta=0}$.
Thus $\ddot\theta=-(12.81/1.20)\sin20^\circ=\boxed{-3.652\,\mathrm{s^{-2}}}$. Upward support acceleration increases restoring effective gravity. If $\ddot Y=-g$, the support is in free fall and the pendulum has no gravitational restoring term. If $\ddot Y=0$, the ordinary pendulum equation returns.
rubricCriteria: Expands the support-bead velocity and retain the cross term involving support speed.
Applies Euler-Lagrange before replacing support acceleration by its value.
Interprets the combination of gravity and upward support acceleration and test free fall.

commonErrors.description: Uses gravity minus upward support acceleration.
commonErrors.consequence: It predicts weaker restoring motion in an upward-accelerating elevator.

commonErrors.description: Drops the kinetic cross term before applying Euler-Lagrange.
commonErrors.consequence: The support acceleration never enters the equation.

problems.flawedProof: Terms containing prescribed support motion can be discarded, so $\ell\ddot\theta+g\sin\theta=0$ for every $Y(t)$.

problems.title: A symmetric-gauge Lagrangian produces the planar gyroscopic force
problems.objective: Symmetric-gauge variation produces the planar gyroscopic force, its rotation sign, and constant kinetic energy.
problems.statement: Consider $L=m(\dot x^2+\dot y^2)/2+(\Gamma/2)(x\dot y-y\dot x)$, with constant $\Gamma$. Derive both Euler-Lagrange equations, prove kinetic energy is constant, and solve the velocity for initial $\mathbf v(0)=v_0\hat x$. For $m=2.00\,\mathrm{kg}$, $\Gamma=6.00\,\mathrm{kg/s}$, and $v_0=4.00\,\mathrm{m/s}$, find the angular frequency and path radius. Check the sign of rotation and the $\Gamma\to0$ limit.
permittedResults: The velocity-linear term contributes no ordinary kinetic energy.
A force perpendicular to velocity does no work.
problems.strategy: First: Differentiate the velocity-linear term with respect to both coordinates and velocities. Next: Combine the equations into a planar rotation of velocity. Finally: Determine orientation from the initial acceleration and evaluate frequency and radius.
hints: Differentiate the velocity-linear term with respect to both coordinates and velocities.
Combine the equations into a planar rotation of velocity.
Determine orientation from the initial acceleration and evaluate frequency and radius.
problems.solution:
For $x$, Euler-Lagrange gives $m\ddot x-\Gamma\dot y=0$; for $y$, $m\ddot y+\Gamma\dot x=0$. Thus $m\dot{\mathbf v}=-\Gamma\hat z\times\mathbf v$. Dotting with velocity proves constant $mv^2/2$. With $\omega=\Gamma/m=3.00\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$ and initial $v_x=v_0$, one obtains $v_x=v_0\cos\omega t$, $v_y=-v_0\sin\omega t$. Initial acceleration points toward $-y$, so rotation is clockwise. The radius is
$R=v_0/\omega=\boxed{1.333\,\mathrm m}$. As $\Gamma\to0$, $\omega\to0$ and the trajectory tends to uniform straight motion over fixed finite times.
rubricCriteria: Differentiates the velocity-linear term with respect to both coordinates and velocities.
Combines the equations into a planar rotation of velocity.
Determines orientation from the initial acceleration and evaluate frequency and radius.

commonErrors.description: Treats the velocity-linear term as an additional potential energy.
commonErrors.consequence: Gyroscopic zero-power structure is mistaken for a time-varying mechanical energy.

commonErrors.description: Reverses the cross-term sign in one Euler-Lagrange equation.
commonErrors.consequence: The resulting accelerations do not form a perpendicular gyroscopic force.

problems.flawedProof: The cross term is a total derivative and contributes nothing, so both accelerations vanish and the radius is infinite even for nonzero $\Gamma$.

problems.title: Routh reduction on a surface of revolution preserves the meridional metric
problems.objective: Routh reduction retains the meridional metric and obtains the centrifugal barrier and planar radial acceleration.
problems.statement: A bead moves freely on a surface of revolution parameterized by meridional coordinate $u$ and azimuth $\phi$, with metric $ds^2=A(u)^2du^2+B(u)^2d\phi^2$. Derive the conserved $p_\phi$ and the one-coordinate Routhian for $u$. For $A=1$, $B(u)=u$ (a plane in polar coordinates), $m=2.00\,\mathrm{kg}$, $p_\phi=8.00\,\mathrm{kg\,m^2/s}$, and $u=4.00\,\mathrm m$, compute the effective barrier and radial acceleration at zero radial speed.
permittedResults: The Routhian is $\mathcal R=L-p_\phi\dot\phi$ after eliminating a cyclic velocity.
$p_\phi=mB(u)^2\dot\phi$.
problems.strategy: First: Solve the cyclic momentum equation for azimuthal speed. Next: Legendre-transform only the cyclic coordinate and keep the meridional kinetic coefficient. Finally: Differentiate the effective barrier with the metric factor and check the planar limit.
hints: Solve the cyclic momentum equation for azimuthal speed.
Legendre-transform only the cyclic coordinate and keep the meridional kinetic coefficient.
Differentiate the effective barrier with the metric factor and check the planar limit.
problems.solution:
The Lagrangian is $L=m[A^2\dot u^2+B^2\dot\phi^2]/2$, and $p_\phi=mB^2\dot\phi$ is constant. Elimination gives
$\boxed{\mathcal R(u,\dot u;p_\phi)=\tfrac12mA^2\dot u^2-\frac{p_\phi^2}{2mB^2}}$.
Thus the effective potential is $p_\phi^2/(2mB^2)$. In the planar case at $u=4$, it is $64/[2(2)(16)]=\boxed{1.00\,\mathrm J}$. The radial equation is $m\ddot u=p_\phi^2/(mu^3)$ at zero radial speed, so $\ddot u=64/[4(64)]=\boxed{0.250\,\mathrm{m/s^2}}$, the coordinate acceleration needed for a straight Cartesian trajectory with tangential motion.
rubricCriteria: Solves the cyclic momentum equation for azimuthal speed.
Legendre-transforms only the cyclic coordinate and keep the meridional kinetic coefficient.
Differentiates the effective barrier with the metric factor and check the planar limit.

commonErrors.description: Substitutes the cyclic velocity into the original Lagrangian without the partial Legendre transform.
commonErrors.consequence: Routhian sign reversal changes centrifugal repulsion into attraction toward the axis.

commonErrors.description: Drops the meridional metric factor in the reduced equation.
commonErrors.consequence: The construction fails on nonplanar surfaces.

problems.flawedProof: Direct substitution gives a positive Routhian term $+p_\phi^2/(2mB^2)$, so angular momentum attracts the bead toward the axis and $\ddot u=-0.250\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$.

problems.title: A rotating hoop bifurcates from one equilibrium into two
problems.objective: Rotating-hoop dynamics locates the pitchfork threshold, classifies all equilibria, and evaluates the stable displaced pair.
problems.statement: A bead moves on a vertical circular hoop of radius $a$ rotating at constant angular speed $\Omega$ about its vertical diameter. Let $\theta$ be measured from the lowest point. Derive the reduced Lagrangian and equilibrium condition. Classify the bottom and top equilibria and find the additional symmetry-related off-bottom equilibria. For $a=0.500\,\mathrm m$, $\Omega=6.00\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$, and $g=9.81\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$, compute their angles and state the threshold.
permittedResults: The bead speed is $a^2(\dot\theta^2+\Omega^2\sin^2\theta)$ under the imposed hoop rotation.
Stability follows from the curvature of the effective potential.
problems.strategy: First: Include both motion along the hoop and imposed azimuthal motion. Next: Factor the equilibrium equation into a sine and a bracket. Finally: Evaluate the bottom curvature and solve the cosine condition with its existence bound.
hints: Include both motion along the hoop and imposed azimuthal motion.
Factor the equilibrium equation into a sine and a bracket.
Evaluate the bottom curvature and solve the cosine condition with its existence bound.
problems.solution:
The Lagrangian is
$L=\tfrac12ma^2(\dot\theta^2+\Omega^2\sin^2\theta)+mga\cos\theta$.
The equation is $a\ddot\theta=\sin\theta(a\Omega^2\cos\theta-g)$. Equilibria satisfy $\sin\theta=0$ or
$\cos\theta=g/(a\Omega^2)$. The bottom is stable when $g-a\Omega^2>0$ and unstable above the threshold $\Omega_c=\sqrt{g/a}$; the top $\theta=\pi$ is unstable for every $\Omega$. Here $a\Omega^2=18.0>9.81$, so
$\theta_*=\pm\arccos(9.81/18.0)=\boxed{\pm0.994\,\mathrm{rad}=\pm56.95^\circ}$,
and these symmetry-related equilibria are stable. The threshold is $\Omega_c=\boxed{4.429\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}}$.
rubricCriteria: Includes both motion along the hoop and imposed azimuthal motion.
Factors the equilibrium equation into a sine and a bracket.
Evaluates the bottom curvature and solve the cosine condition with its existence bound.

commonErrors.description: Uses a cosine-squared rotational speed term instead of sine-squared.
commonErrors.consequence: The centrifugal effect is assigned to the rotation axis rather than distance from it.

commonErrors.description: Declares nonzero equilibria for every angular speed.
commonErrors.consequence: Cosine existence bounds are ignored, creating displaced equilibria below the bifurcation threshold.

problems.flawedProof: Equilibrium requires $\cos\theta=a\Omega^2/g$, giving no real nonzero angle here because the ratio exceeds one. The bottom always remains stable.

problems.title: Two rope constraints reduce a movable-pulley network to a coupled mass metric
problems.objective: Holonomic rope elimination builds the coupled kinetic metric of a movable-pulley network, solves its accelerations, and recovers both tension relations.
problems.statement:
An ideal fixed pulley carries rope 1. Mass $m_1$ hangs from one end; the other end supports the axle of a massless movable pulley. Rope 2 passes over the movable pulley, with masses $m_2$ and $m_3$ hanging from its two ends. All rope segments are vertical, pulleys and ropes are massless, ropes do not slip, and downward coordinates are $y_1,y_P,y_2,y_3$ for $m_1$, the movable-pulley axle, $m_2$, and $m_3$.

Write both fixed-length constraints. Choose $q_1=y_1$ and $q_2=y_2$ as independent coordinates, eliminate $y_P$ and $y_3$, and derive the reduced Lagrangian. Obtain the coupled $2\times2$ acceleration system, showing explicitly where its off-diagonal kinetic term comes from.

For $m_1=2.00\,\mathrm{kg}$, $m_2=3.00\,\mathrm{kg}$, $m_3=1.00\,\mathrm{kg}$, and $g=9.81\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$, compute $\ddot y_1,\ddot y_P,\ddot y_2,\ddot y_3$. Recover tensions $T_1$ and $T_2$ and verify the massless movable-pulley condition. Audit both acceleration-level constraints.
permittedResults: For an ideal massless rope, each rope has uniform tension; a massless pulley has zero net force.
problems.strategy: Differentiate the two rope-length equations only after eliminating dependent coordinates. Build kinetic energy from all three mass velocities, derive the reduced mass matrix, and then use individual Newton equations solely as a reaction-force audit.
hints: The constraints may be written $y_1+y_P=C_1$ and $y_2+y_3-2y_P=C_2$.
With $q_1=y_1$ and $q_2=y_2$, $\dot y_P=-\dot q_1$ and $\dot y_3=-2\dot q_1-\dot q_2$.
For the stated masses, the reduced matrix is $\begin{pmatrix}6&2\\2&4\end{pmatrix}\,\mathrm{kg}$.
problems.solution:
The fixed lengths give
$$
y_1+y_P=C_1,
\qquad
y_2+y_3-2y_P=C_2.
$$
Ignoring additive constants,
$$
y_P=-q_1,
\qquad
y_3=-2q_1-q_2.
$$
Therefore
$$
T=\frac12m_1\dot q_1^2+\frac12m_2\dot q_2^2
+\frac12m_3(2\dot q_1+\dot q_2)^2,
$$
while, because downward coordinates have gravitational potential $-mgy$,
$$
L=T+g[(m_1-2m_3)q_1+(m_2-m_3)q_2]+\text{constant}.
$$
Euler--Lagrange yields
$$
\boxed{
\begin{pmatrix}
m_1+4m_3&2m_3\\
2m_3&m_2+m_3
\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix}\ddot q_1\\\ddot q_2\end{pmatrix}
=g\begin{pmatrix}m_1-2m_3\\m_2-m_3\end{pmatrix}}.
$$
The off-diagonal entries come from the shared velocity of $m_3$, not from an added force.

For the stated masses,
$$
\begin{pmatrix}6&2\\2&4\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix}\ddot q_1\\\ddot q_2\end{pmatrix}
=\begin{pmatrix}0\\19.62\end{pmatrix}\,\mathrm N.
$$
Solving gives
$$
\boxed{\ddot y_1=\ddot q_1=-1.962\,\mathrm{m/s^2}},
\qquad
\boxed{\ddot y_2=\ddot q_2=5.886\,\mathrm{m/s^2}}.
$$
The eliminated coordinates give
$$
\boxed{\ddot y_P=1.962\,\mathrm{m/s^2}},
\qquad
\boxed{\ddot y_3=-2\ddot q_1-\ddot q_2=-1.962\,\mathrm{m/s^2}}.
$$

For $m_1$, $m_1\ddot y_1=m_1g-T_1$, so
$$
T_1=2.00[9.81-(-1.962)]=\boxed{23.544\,\mathrm N}.
$$
For $m_2$, $m_2\ddot y_2=m_2g-T_2$, hence
$$
T_2=3.00(9.81-5.886)=\boxed{11.772\,\mathrm N}.
$$
Thus $T_1=2T_2$, exactly the zero-net-force condition on the massless movable pulley. Finally,
$\ddot y_1+\ddot y_P=0$ and
$\ddot y_2+\ddot y_3-2\ddot y_P=0$, so both acceleration constraints close numerically.
rubricCriteria: Writes and eliminates both rope constraints with consistent downward-coordinate signs.
Builds the coupled reduced kinetic energy and derives the exact mass-matrix equation.
Solves all four accelerations, recovers both tensions, and verifies pulley force balance and constraints.

commonErrors.description: Uses $y_2+y_3-y_P=\text{constant}$ for the rope around the movable pulley.
commonErrors.consequence: One moving support segment is omitted, corrupting every dependent velocity and acceleration.

commonErrors.description: Adds three independent one-mass kinetic energies after eliminating coordinates but drops the shared cross term.
commonErrors.consequence: The reduced mass matrix becomes diagonal and cannot reproduce the rope-coupled motion.

problems.flawedProof: Rope 2 has length $y_2+y_3-y_P$, so $y_3=-q_1-q_2$. Each mass then supplies one uncoupled equation, and the two rope tensions must be equal because every pulley is ideal.

problems.title: A plane constraint multiplier is the normal reaction
problems.objective: Multiplier variation identifies the plane reaction, cancels only normal forcing, and preserves tangential acceleration.
problems.statement: A particle of mass $m$ moves under constant force $\mathbf f$ while constrained to the plane $\mathbf n\cdot\mathbf r=d$, where $\mathbf n$ is a unit normal. Use the augmented Lagrangian $L_*=m\dot{\mathbf r}^2/2+\mathbf f\cdot\mathbf r+\lambda(\mathbf n\cdot\mathbf r-d)$ to derive the motion and solve for $\lambda$. For $m=2.00\,\mathrm{kg}$, $\mathbf n=(0,0,1)$, and $\mathbf f=(3.00,-2.00,-5.00)\,\mathrm N$, find acceleration and constraint force. Check the case of a force tangent to the plane.
permittedResults: Twice differentiating a fixed plane constraint gives $\mathbf n\cdot\ddot{\mathbf r}=0$.
problems.strategy: First: Vary the particle position and the multiplier independently. Next: Project the vector equation along the plane normal to enforce zero normal acceleration. Finally: Separate tangential applied force from normal reaction and check force units and sign.
hints: Vary the particle position and the multiplier independently.
Project the vector equation along the plane normal to enforce zero normal acceleration.
Separate tangential applied force from normal reaction and check force units and sign.
problems.solution:
Variation gives $m\ddot{\mathbf r}=\mathbf f+\lambda\mathbf n$ and the plane constraint. Dotting with $\mathbf n$ yields $0=\mathbf n\cdot\mathbf f+\lambda$, so
$\boxed{\lambda=-\mathbf n\cdot\mathbf f}$. Here $\lambda=+5.00\,\mathrm N$, the constraint force is $(0,0,5.00)\,\mathrm N$, and the net force is $(3,-2,0)\,\mathrm N$. Thus
$\boxed{\ddot{\mathbf r}=(1.50,-1.00,0)\,\mathrm{m/s^2}}$. If the applied force is tangent, its normal component is zero, $\lambda=0$, and the plane need exert no reaction.
rubricCriteria: Varies the particle position and the multiplier independently.
Projects the vector equation along the plane normal to enforce zero normal acceleration.
Separates tangential applied force from normal reaction and check force units and sign.

commonErrors.description: Sets the multiplier equal to the applied normal component without the opposing sign.
commonErrors.consequence: The constraint doubles rather than cancels normal acceleration.

commonErrors.description: Removes the full applied force rather than only its normal component.
commonErrors.consequence: Tangential acceleration is incorrectly suppressed.

problems.flawedProof: The multiplier equals $-5.00\,\mathrm N$, so the constraint force adds another downward $5.00\,\mathrm N$ and acceleration has a $-5.00\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$ normal component.

problems.title: A time-dependent uniform force has a conserved shifted momentum
problems.objective: Time-integrated forcing defines a conserved shifted momentum and determines the exact driven velocity.
problems.statement: A particle on a line has $L=m\dot q^2/2+F(t)q$. Let $J(t)$ satisfy $\dot J=F(t)$ and $J(0)=0$. Derive the Euler-Lagrange equation and prove that $p-J(t)$ is conserved even though ordinary momentum is not. For $m=2.00\,\mathrm{kg}$, $F(t)=6.00(t/1.00\,\mathrm s)\,\mathrm N$, and $\dot q(0)=1.00\,\mathrm{m/s}$, find $\dot q(3.00\,\mathrm s)$ and the conserved shifted momentum.
permittedResults: Canonical momentum is $p=m\dot q$.
An antiderivative of the applied force has impulse units.
problems.strategy: First: Apply Euler-Lagrange while retaining the explicit time dependence of the applied force. Next: Differentiate the proposed shifted momentum. Finally: Integrate the force with its time scale and evaluate velocity from impulse-momentum.
hints: Apply Euler-Lagrange while retaining the explicit time dependence of the applied force.
Differentiate the proposed shifted momentum.
Integrate the force with its time scale and evaluate velocity from impulse-momentum.
problems.solution:
Euler-Lagrange gives $\dot p=F(t)$. Therefore
$d[p-J(t)]/dt=F-\dot J=0$, so $\boxed{p-J(t)=p(0)}$. Here
$J(t)=\int_0^t6(s/1\,\mathrm s)ds=3t^2/(1\,\mathrm s)\,\mathrm{N}$, which at $t=3\,\mathrm s$ is $27.0\,\mathrm{N\,s}$. Initial momentum is $2.00\,\mathrm{kg\,m/s}$, so final momentum is $29.0\,\mathrm{kg\,m/s}$ and
$\boxed{\dot q(3)=14.5\,\mathrm{m/s}}$. The conserved shifted momentum is $\boxed{2.00\,\mathrm{kg\,m/s}}$. If $F\to0$, $J\to0$ and ordinary momentum conservation returns.
rubricCriteria: Applies Euler-Lagrange while retaining the explicit time dependence of the applied force.
Differentiates the proposed shifted momentum.
Integrates the force with its time scale and evaluate velocity from impulse-momentum.

commonErrors.description: Declares canonical momentum conserved because the kinetic term has no coordinate dependence.
commonErrors.consequence: Coordinate-linear forcing is overlooked and canonical momentum is falsely declared constant.

commonErrors.description: Integrates a force linear in time as another linear function.
commonErrors.consequence: The impulse and final speed are too small.

problems.flawedProof: The coordinate is cyclic, so $m\dot q=2.00\,\mathrm{kg\,m/s}$ remains constant and the speed stays $1.00\,\mathrm{m/s}$.

problems.title: A conical pendulum follows from a constrained stationary latitude
problems.objective: Conical-pendulum balance fixes angular rate, tension, and both small-angle and horizontal limits.
problems.statement: Using the spherical-pendulum Lagrangian with polar angle $\theta$ measured from downward vertical, derive the condition for a conical pendulum with constant $\theta=\theta_0\ne0$ and constant azimuthal rate $\Omega$. For mass $m=2.00\,\mathrm{kg}$, $\ell=1.50\,\mathrm m$, and $\theta_0=40.0^\circ$, compute $\Omega$, the period, and string tension. Verify the small-angle and horizontal-limit behavior.
permittedResults: The spherical-pendulum equation is $\ddot\theta-\sin\theta\cos\theta\dot\phi^2+(g/\ell)\sin\theta=0$.
Radial force balance may be used to find tension after the motion is known.
problems.strategy: First: Set polar acceleration and polar velocity to zero in the angular equation without dividing by a potentially zero sine too early. Next: Solve the remaining balance for azimuthal rate and period. Finally: Use vertical force balance for tension and inspect both angular limits.
hints: Set polar acceleration and polar velocity to zero in the angular equation without dividing by a potentially zero sine too early.
Solve the remaining balance for azimuthal rate and period.
Use vertical force balance for tension and inspect both angular limits.
problems.solution:
For $\theta_0\ne0$, the stationary-latitude equation gives
$-\sin\theta_0\cos\theta_0\Omega^2+(g/\ell)\sin\theta_0=0$, hence
$\boxed{\Omega^2=g/(\ell\cos\theta_0)}$.
Numerically, $\Omega=\sqrt{9.81/[1.5\cos40^\circ]}=\boxed{2.923\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}}$ and $P=2\pi/\Omega=\boxed{2.150\,\mathrm s}$. Vertical balance gives $T\cos\theta_0=mg$, so $T=mg/\cos\theta_0=\boxed{25.61\,\mathrm N}$. As $\theta_0\to0$, $\Omega\to\sqrt{g/\ell}$, although the zero-radius orbit degenerates. As $\theta_0\to\pi/2$, required rate and tension diverge, so a finite-rate horizontal conical pendulum is impossible.
rubricCriteria: Sets polar acceleration and polar velocity to zero in the angular equation without dividing by a potentially zero sine too early.
Solves the remaining balance for azimuthal rate and period.
Uses vertical force balance for tension and inspect both angular limits.

commonErrors.description: Uses sine instead of cosine in the conical-rate denominator.
commonErrors.consequence: The small-angle and horizontal limits are reversed.

commonErrors.description: Sets tension equal to weight at nonzero cone angle.
commonErrors.consequence: It fails vertical force balance and understates the reaction.

problems.flawedProof: The rate is $\Omega^2=g/(\ell\sin\theta_0)$ and tension is always $mg$. Thus a horizontal conical pendulum has finite rate.

problems.title: The brachistochrone first integral generates a cycloid
problems.objective: Brachistochrone variation yields the Beltrami first integral, cycloidal parametrization, and finite cusp travel time.
problems.statement: Take $y$ positive downward from a release point and let a frictionless bead start from rest. Derive the travel-time functional for a graph $y(x)$, use the Beltrami identity to obtain $y(1+y'^2)=2a$, and verify that $x=a(\theta-\sin\theta)$, $y=a(1-\cos\theta)$ solves it. For the endpoint $\theta=\pi$ with $a=1.00\,\mathrm m$, compute horizontal drop, vertical drop, and travel time. State the endpoint and cusp caveats.
permittedResults: Energy gives speed $v=\sqrt{2gy}$.
For an autonomous integrand $f(y,y')$, $f-y'f_{y'}$ is constant.
problems.strategy: First: Write time as path length divided by the energy-determined speed. Next: Apply the Beltrami identity before attempting to solve the nonlinear differential equation. Finally: Substitute the cycloidal parameterization and integrate $dt$ with the release cusp handled as a limit.
hints: Write time as path length divided by the energy-determined speed.
Apply the Beltrami identity before attempting to solve the nonlinear differential equation.
Substitute the cycloidal parameterization and integrate $dt$ with the release cusp handled as a limit.
problems.solution:
Travel time is $T=\int\sqrt{1+y'^2}/\sqrt{2gy}\,dx$. Beltrami gives $[\sqrt{2gy}\sqrt{1+y'^2}]^{-1}=\text{constant}$, equivalently $\boxed{y(1+y'^2)=2a}$. For the cycloid, $dx/d\theta=a(1-\cos\theta)$, $dy/d\theta=a\sin\theta$, so $y'=\sin\theta/(1-\cos\theta)$ and the identity holds. Also $ds=2a\sin(\theta/2)d\theta$ and $v=2\sqrt{ag}\sin(\theta/2)$, hence $dt=\sqrt{a/g}\,d\theta$. At $\theta=\pi$,
$x=\boxed{\pi\,\mathrm m}$, $y=\boxed{2.00\,\mathrm m}$, and $T=\pi\sqrt{1/9.81}=\boxed{1.003\,\mathrm s}$. The derivation assumes a monotone downward branch; the zero-speed cusp is interpreted by an integrable limiting process and endpoint transversality is not free when endpoints are fixed.
rubricCriteria: Writes time as path length divided by the energy-determined speed.
Applies the Beltrami identity before attempting to solve the nonlinear differential equation.
Substitutes the cycloidal parameterization and integrate $dt$ with the release cusp handled as a limit.

commonErrors.description: Minimizes geometric path length instead of travel time weighted by inverse speed.
commonErrors.consequence: Travel-time weighting is lost and the wrong straight-line extremal is selected.

commonErrors.description: Treats the release cusp's zero speed as a divergent travel time.
commonErrors.consequence: Release-cusp integrability is missed even though path length and speed vanish compatibly.

problems.flawedProof: The quickest path minimizes $\int ds$, so it is the straight chord. Because $v=0$ at release, the cycloid takes infinite time to start.

problems.title: The fixed-length hanging chain extremal is a catenary
problems.objective: Length-constrained energy variation derives the catenary, interprets horizontal tension, and recovers the parabolic small-sag limit.
problems.statement: A uniform flexible chain with fixed endpoints and fixed length minimizes gravitational potential energy. Using $y$ upward, introduce a length multiplier and derive the catenary family. Choose the symmetric member with lowest point at $(0,0)$ and scale $a=2.00\,\mathrm m$. Find $y$ and slope at $x=2.00\,\mathrm m$. Explain the roles of the multiplier, horizontal tension, and the small-sag limit.
permittedResults: The augmented integrand may be written $(y+\lambda)\sqrt{1+y'^2}$.
The Beltrami identity applies because the integrand has no explicit $x$.
problems.strategy: First: Combine potential-energy and fixed-length integrands before varying. Next: Use the Beltrami constant to solve for slope as a function of height. Finally: Set symmetry constants from the lowest point and evaluate the hyperbolic functions.
hints: Combine potential-energy and fixed-length integrands before varying.
Use the Beltrami constant to solve for slope as a function of height.
Set symmetry constants from the lowest point and evaluate the hyperbolic functions.
problems.solution:
Beltrami gives
$(y+\lambda)/\sqrt{1+y'^2}=a$, where $a>0$ is constant. Thus $y'^2=(y+\lambda)^2/a^2-1$, whose solution is
$y+\lambda=a\cosh[(x-x_0)/a]$. For a symmetric lowest point at $(0,0)$, $x_0=0$ and $\lambda=a$, so
$\boxed{y=a[\cosh(x/a)-1]}$. At $a=2$ and $x=2$,
$y=2(\cosh1-1)=\boxed{1.086\,\mathrm m}$ and $y'=\sinh1=\boxed{1.175}$. The multiplier enforces total length; $a$ is proportional to horizontal tension divided by weight per length. For $|x|\ll a$, $y\approx x^2/(2a)$, the parabolic small-sag limit.
rubricCriteria: Combines potential-energy and fixed-length integrands before varying.
Uses the Beltrami constant to solve for slope as a function of height.
Sets symmetry constants from the lowest point and evaluate the hyperbolic functions.

commonErrors.description: Varies gravitational potential without enforcing fixed chain length.
commonErrors.consequence: The minimizer can lower energy by changing the amount of chain.

commonErrors.description: Uses a trigonometric cosine instead of a hyperbolic cosine.
commonErrors.consequence: The profile fails the first integral and has the wrong convexity.

problems.flawedProof: Fixed length adds no multiplier because endpoints already determine length. The solution is $y=a[1-\cos(x/a)]$, a circular arc.

problems.title: A multiplier proof shows every spherical free geodesic is a great circle
problems.objective: Spherical multiplier dynamics proves force-free constrained paths are great circles and excludes unsupported small circles.
problems.statement: A free particle is constrained by $\mathbf r^2=R^2$. Use $L_*=m\dot{\mathbf r}^2/2+\lambda(\mathbf r^2-R^2)/2$ to derive the multiplier and show that the trajectory lies in a fixed plane through the origin. For $m=1.00\,\mathrm{kg}$, $R=2.00\,\mathrm m$, and speed $v=3.00\,\mathrm{m/s}$, find the multiplier and angular speed around the great circle. Explain why a small circle at fixed nonzero latitude is not a force-free geodesic.
permittedResults: Differentiating $\mathbf r^2=R^2$ twice gives $\mathbf r\cdot\ddot{\mathbf r}=-v^2$.
A constant vector $\mathbf r\times\dot{\mathbf r}$ fixes an orbital plane.
problems.strategy: First: Vary position and multiplier independently, then project the equation along the radius. Next: Use the differentiated constraint to solve the multiplier sign. Finally: Prove planarity from angular momentum and evaluate the constant-speed circular rate.
hints: Vary position and multiplier independently, then project the equation along the radius.
Use the differentiated constraint to solve the multiplier sign.
Prove planarity from angular momentum and evaluate the constant-speed circular rate.
problems.solution:
Variation gives $m\ddot{\mathbf r}=\lambda\mathbf r$. Dotting with $\mathbf r$ and using $\mathbf r\cdot\ddot{\mathbf r}=-v^2$ yields
$\boxed{\lambda=-mv^2/R^2}$. Therefore $\ddot{\mathbf r}=-(v^2/R^2)\mathbf r$. Also $d(\mathbf r\times m\dot{\mathbf r})/dt=\mathbf r\times\lambda\mathbf r=0$, so the motion stays in the plane perpendicular to a fixed angular momentum vector; its intersection with the sphere is a great circle. Numerically, $\lambda=-1(3^2)/(2^2)=\boxed{-2.25\,\mathrm{N/m}}$ and angular speed is $v/R=\boxed{1.50\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}}$. A small circle requires an acceleration component within the tangent plane toward its own center, which the purely radial constraint force cannot supply.
rubricCriteria: Varies position and multiplier independently, then project the equation along the radius.
Uses the differentiated constraint to solve the multiplier sign.
Proves planarity from angular momentum and evaluate the constant-speed circular rate.

commonErrors.description: Assigns a positive multiplier for inward centripetal acceleration.
commonErrors.consequence: The constraint force points outward and cannot maintain the sphere.

commonErrors.description: Infers only that the path is circular, without proving its plane passes through the sphere center.
commonErrors.consequence: Small circles are incorrectly admitted as free geodesics.

problems.flawedProof: The multiplier is positive $mv^2/R^2$, and any circle drawn on a sphere is a free geodesic because its radius is constant.

problems.title: Lagrange-d'Alembert motion of a knife edge is uniform circular drift
problems.objective: Knife-edge d'Alembert equations determine the lateral reaction, constant speeds, and circular center path.
problems.statement: A planar knife edge has configuration $(x,y,\theta)$, kinetic energy $m(\dot x^2+\dot y^2)/2+I\dot\theta^2/2$, and no lateral-slip constraint $-\sin\theta\dot x+\cos\theta\dot y=0$. Apply Lagrange-d'Alembert with multiplier reaction along the forbidden lateral direction. Derive the multiplier, prove forward speed and angular speed are constant, and identify the path. For $m=2.00\,\mathrm{kg}$, forward speed $v=3.00\,\mathrm{m/s}$, and $\dot\theta=0.500\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$, compute multiplier magnitude and turning radius.
permittedResults: The admissible velocity is $(\dot x,\dot y)=v(\cos\theta,\sin\theta)$.
An ideal nonholonomic reaction does zero power on admissible velocity.
problems.strategy: First: Write multiplier forces using the constraint covector and the free rotational equation. Next: Differentiate the velocity constraint and insert the multiplier accelerations. Finally: Project acceleration along and perpendicular to the blade to obtain constants and path radius.
hints: Write multiplier forces using the constraint covector and the free rotational equation.
Differentiate the velocity constraint and insert the multiplier accelerations.
Project acceleration along and perpendicular to the blade to obtain constants and path radius.
problems.solution:
Lagrange-d'Alembert gives $m\ddot x=-\lambda\sin\theta$, $m\ddot y=\lambda\cos\theta$, and $I\ddot\theta=0$. Differentiating the constraint and using $(\dot x,\dot y)=v(\cos\theta,\sin\theta)$ yields $-v\dot\theta+\lambda/m=0$, so
$\boxed{\lambda=mv\dot\theta}$. Tangential projection gives $\dot v=0$, while $\dot\theta$ is constant. The contact point therefore follows a circle of radius $R=v/|\dot\theta|$. Numerically, $\lambda=2(3)(0.5)=\boxed{3.00\,\mathrm N}$ and $R=3/0.5=\boxed{6.00\,\mathrm m}$. If $\dot\theta\to0$, reaction vanishes and the path becomes straight.
rubricCriteria: Writes multiplier forces using the constraint covector and the free rotational equation.
Differentiates the velocity constraint and insert the multiplier accelerations.
Projects acceleration along and perpendicular to the blade to obtain constants and path radius.

commonErrors.description: Treats the velocity constraint as a fixed positional curve.
commonErrors.consequence: It removes valid knife-edge motions and obtains the wrong reaction.

commonErrors.description: Projects the multiplier along the blade rather than laterally.
commonErrors.consequence: The ideal reaction does work and changes forward speed.

problems.flawedProof: The constraint integrates to $-x\sin\theta+y\cos\theta=0$, so the blade remains on one fixed line and the multiplier is zero for every motion.

problems.title: Routh reduction finds the steady latitude on a gravitational cone
problems.objective: Conical Routh reduction finds the stable steady latitude, azimuthal rate, and flat-cone boundary.
problems.statement: A bead moves on the cone $z=cr$ in gravity, with cylindrical coordinates $(r,\phi)$. Derive the Lagrangian, reduce the cyclic azimuth, and find the radius of a steady circular orbit at fixed angular momentum $p_\phi$. For $m=1.00\,\mathrm{kg}$, $c=0.500$, $p_\phi=4.00\,\mathrm{kg\,m^2/s}$, and $g=9.81\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$, compute the radius and azimuthal rate. Prove radial stability and state the $c\to0^+$ behavior.
permittedResults: The cone metric gives $v^2=(1+c^2)\dot r^2+r^2\dot\phi^2$.
The reduced effective potential is $p_\phi^2/(2mr^2)+mgcr$.
problems.strategy: First: Use the surface metric and identify azimuthal momentum. Next: Differentiate the reduced effective potential to obtain the balance radius. Finally: Evaluate its second derivative and inspect flattening of the cone.
hints: Use the surface metric and identify azimuthal momentum.
Differentiate the reduced effective potential to obtain the balance radius.
Evaluate its second derivative and inspect flattening of the cone.
problems.solution:
The Lagrangian is $L=m[(1+c^2)\dot r^2+r^2\dot\phi^2]/2-mgcr$, with $p_\phi=mr^2\dot\phi$. The reduced potential is
$U_{\rm eff}=p_\phi^2/(2mr^2)+mgcr$. Steady radius obeys
$-p_\phi^2/(mr^3)+mgc=0$, hence
$\boxed{r_*=[p_\phi^2/(m^2gc)]^{1/3}}$.
Numerically, $r_*=[16/4.905]^{1/3}=\boxed{1.483\,\mathrm m}$ and $\dot\phi=p_\phi/(mr_*^2)=\boxed{1.819\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}}$. Since $U_{\rm eff}''=3p_\phi^2/(mr^4)>0$, the radial equilibrium is stable. As $c\to0^+$, gravity loses its along-surface component and $r_*$ diverges for fixed nonzero angular momentum.
rubricCriteria: Uses the surface metric and identify azimuthal momentum.
Differentiates the reduced effective potential to obtain the balance radius.
Evaluates its second derivative and inspect flattening of the cone.

commonErrors.description: Uses the cone slant factor in the azimuthal inertia.
commonErrors.consequence: It changes the conserved angular momentum and steady radius incorrectly.

commonErrors.description: Chooses the maximum rather than minimum of the effective potential.
commonErrors.consequence: It misclassifies a stable steady orbit as unstable.

problems.flawedProof: The steady radius is $p_\phi^2/(m^2gc)$ without a cube root, and the negative centrifugal curvature makes it unstable.

problems.title: Polar gauge separates canonical from mechanical angular momentum
problems.objective: Uniform-field dynamics in polar coordinates derives the velocity-linear Lagrangian, cyclic canonical momentum, radial Lorentz force, and gauge-invariant mechanical content.
problems.statement:
A particle of mass $m$ and charge $q$ moves in the plane perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field $\mathbf B=B\hat{\mathbf z}$. In symmetric polar gauge,
$$
\mathbf A=\frac12Br\,\hat{\boldsymbol\phi},
\qquad \Phi=0.
$$
Derive the polar-coordinate Lagrangian and both Euler--Lagrange equations. Identify the cyclic canonical angular momentum and express the gauge-invariant mechanical angular momentum in terms of it. Verify the radial and azimuthal Lorentz-force components directly.

For $m=2.00\,\mathrm{kg}$, $q=1.00\,\mathrm C$, $B=4.00\,\mathrm T$, $r=0.500\,\mathrm m$, $\dot r=0$, and $\dot\phi=-1.00\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$, compute canonical angular momentum, mechanical angular momentum, radial acceleration, and energy. Find the nonzero angular rate for a circle centered at the coordinate origin.

Finally let $\mathbf A' =\mathbf A+\nabla\chi$. State how the reduced canonical momentum changes when $\chi(r,\phi,t)$ depends on $\phi$, and explain which angular momentum and trajectory statements are gauge invariant.
permittedResults: For electromagnetic potentials, $L=T+q\mathbf A\cdot\mathbf v-q\Phi$ and a gauge change adds $q\,d\chi/dt$.
problems.strategy: Insert the polar velocity into the vector-potential coupling before differentiating. Keep canonical and mechanical angular momentum distinct, then use a total-derivative gauge change to identify which quantity shifts.
hints: Here $q\mathbf A\cdot\mathbf v=qBr^2\dot\phi/2$.
The mechanical angular momentum is $mr^2\dot\phi=p_\phi-qBr^2/2$.
A centered nonzero circular orbit satisfies $\dot\phi(\dot\phi+qB/m)=0$.
problems.solution:
The Lagrangian is
$$
\boxed{L=\frac12m(\dot r^2+r^2\dot\phi^2)
+\frac12qBr^2\dot\phi}.
$$
The radial equation is
$$
\boxed{m\ddot r=mr\dot\phi^2+qBr\dot\phi},
$$
and cyclicity of $\phi$ gives
$$
\boxed{p_\phi=mr^2\dot\phi+\frac12qBr^2=\text{constant}}.
$$
Equivalently,
$$
\frac d{dt}(mr^2\dot\phi)=-qBr\dot r.
$$
Directly, $q\mathbf v\times\mathbf B$ has radial component
$qBr\dot\phi$ and azimuthal component $-qB\dot r$, matching both equations. The gauge-invariant mechanical angular momentum is
$$
\boxed{L_z^{\rm mech}=mr^2\dot\phi=p_\phi-\frac12qBr^2}.
$$

Numerically,
$$
p_\phi=2.00(0.500)^2(-1.00)
+\frac12(1.00)(4.00)(0.500)^2
=\boxed{0},
$$
while
$$
\boxed{L_z^{\rm mech}=-0.500\,\mathrm{kg\,m^2/s}}.
$$
The radial acceleration is
$$
\ddot r=r\dot\phi^2+\frac{qB}{m}r\dot\phi
=0.500-1.000
=\boxed{-0.500\,\mathrm{m/s^2}}.
$$
The energy contains no velocity-linear term:
$$
E=\frac12m(\dot r^2+r^2\dot\phi^2)
=\boxed{0.250\,\mathrm J}.
$$
For a centered circle with $\dot r=\ddot r=0$, the nonzero branch is
$$
\boxed{\dot\phi=-qB/m=-2.00\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}}.
$$

Under $\mathbf A' =\mathbf A+\nabla\chi$, the Lagrangian changes by
$q\,d\chi/dt$, so
$$
\boxed{p_\phi'=p_\phi+q\frac{\partial\chi}{\partial\phi}}.
$$
Canonical momentum can therefore shift with gauge. Mechanical momentum, Lorentz force, energy for the static scalar-potential choice, and physical trajectories remain gauge invariant when all potentials and boundary terms are transformed consistently.
rubricCriteria: Derives the polar velocity coupling and both Lorentz-consistent Euler--Lagrange equations.
Separates cyclic canonical momentum from gauge-invariant mechanical angular momentum.
Computes the stated quantities and centered-circle rate, then tracks the canonical gauge shift.

commonErrors.description: Treats $p_\phi$ as the mechanical angular momentum and drops the vector-potential term.
commonErrors.consequence: The stated moving particle is assigned zero physical angular momentum because its canonical momentum vanishes.

commonErrors.description: Includes $q\mathbf A\cdot\mathbf v$ as an extra positive term in mechanical energy.
commonErrors.consequence: The velocity-linear gauge contribution makes the claimed energy gauge dependent.

problems.flawedProof: Because $\phi$ is cyclic, $mr^2\dot\phi$ is conserved and equals $p_\phi=0$. The particle therefore has no angular momentum or radial acceleration, while $q\mathbf A\cdot\mathbf v$ lowers its energy.

problems.title: Galilean boosts are quasi-symmetries of the free-particle action
problems.objective: Boost quasi-symmetry and its boundary term generate the correct center-of-mass Noether charge.
problems.statement: For a free particle $L=m\dot q^2/2$, consider the infinitesimal boost $\delta q=\epsilon t$. Show that $\delta L$ is a total time derivative rather than zero, and derive the corresponding Noether conserved quantity. For $m=2.00\,\mathrm{kg}$, $q(0)=3.00\,\mathrm m$, and $\dot q=4.00\,\mathrm{m/s}$, evaluate the conserved quantity and verify it at $t=5.00\,\mathrm s$. Explain why omitting the boundary term gives the wrong result.
permittedResults: For a quasi-symmetry with $\delta L=dF/dt$, Noether charge is $p\,\delta q-F$.
problems.strategy: First: Vary velocity under the time-dependent coordinate displacement. Next: Express the Lagrangian variation as the derivative of a coordinate-dependent boundary function. Finally: Construct the charge, choose a sign convention, and verify it along the explicit straight trajectory.
hints: Vary velocity under the time-dependent coordinate displacement.
Express the Lagrangian variation as the derivative of a coordinate-dependent boundary function.
Construct the charge, choose a sign convention, and verify it along the explicit straight trajectory.
problems.solution:
The boost gives $\delta\dot q=\epsilon$, so $\delta L=m\dot q\epsilon=d(mq\epsilon)/dt$. Thus $F=mq\epsilon$. Dividing the Noether charge by $-\epsilon$ gives the equivalent conserved quantity
$\boxed{K=mq-tp=m(q-t\dot q)}$.
Initially $K=2(3)=\boxed{6.00\,\mathrm{kg\,m}}$. At $t=5$, $q=3+4(5)=23\,\mathrm m$ and $p=8\,\mathrm{kg\,m/s}$, so $K=2(23)-5(8)=6.00\,\mathrm{kg\,m}$. If the boundary term were omitted, one would use $pt$, which is not conserved. The charge fixes the intercept of the inertial worldline.
rubricCriteria: Varies velocity under the time-dependent coordinate displacement.
Expresses the Lagrangian variation as the derivative of a coordinate-dependent boundary function.
Constructs the charge, choose a sign convention, and verify it along the explicit straight trajectory.

commonErrors.description: Requires the free Lagrangian to be strictly invariant under a boost.
commonErrors.consequence: It rejects a valid action quasi-symmetry whose variation is a boundary term.

commonErrors.description: Uses momentum times time alone as the Noether charge.
commonErrors.consequence: Boundary-term omission leaves momentum times time, which grows along the free trajectory.

problems.flawedProof: Since $\delta L=m\dot q\epsilon$ is nonzero, a boost is not a symmetry and there is no conserved charge.

problems.title: Horizontal pivot acceleration drives a pendulum through a cosine torque
problems.objective: Horizontal support acceleration supplies the pendulum cosine torque and the opposite-leaning static equilibrium.
problems.statement: A pendulum support has prescribed horizontal coordinate $X(t)$, with $x=X+\ell\sin\theta$ and $y=-\ell\cos\theta$. Derive the exact equation for $\theta$. For $\ell=1.00\,\mathrm m$, $\theta=30.0^\circ$, $\dot\theta=0$, and support acceleration $\ddot X=+4.00\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$, compute $\ddot\theta$. Determine the static angle in a frame with constant support acceleration and check both zero-drive and zero-gravity limits.
permittedResults: Terms depending only on prescribed support motion may be dropped after the full kinetic energy is expanded.
A constant-acceleration frame has effective gravity vector opposite the frame acceleration plus downward gravity.
problems.strategy: First: Retain the kinetic cross term between support speed and angular velocity. Next: Apply Euler-Lagrange so support acceleration appears after differentiating that cross term. Finally: Solve static balance from the sine-cosine equation and inspect limiting force directions.
hints: Retain the kinetic cross term between support speed and angular velocity.
Apply Euler-Lagrange so support acceleration appears after differentiating that cross term.
Solve static balance from the sine-cosine equation and inspect limiting force directions.
problems.solution:
Up to time-only terms,
$L=\tfrac12m\ell^2\dot\theta^2+m\ell\dot X\cos\theta\dot\theta+mg\ell\cos\theta$.
Euler-Lagrange gives
$\boxed{\ell\ddot\theta+g\sin\theta+\ddot X\cos\theta=0}$.
At the stated instant,
$\ddot\theta=-[9.81(0.5)+4(\sqrt3/2)]/1=\boxed{-8.369\,\mathrm{s^{-2}}}$. Static balance satisfies $\tan\theta_*=-\ddot X/g$, so for positive rightward support acceleration the bob leans left. If $\ddot X\to0$, $\theta_*=0$. If $g\to0$ with nonzero acceleration, the stable string direction becomes horizontal opposite the frame acceleration.
rubricCriteria: Retains the kinetic cross term between support speed and angular velocity.
Applies Euler-Lagrange so support acceleration appears after differentiating that cross term.
Solves static balance from the sine-cosine equation and inspect limiting force directions.

commonErrors.description: Uses a sine rather than cosine factor for the horizontal inertial torque.
commonErrors.consequence: The equation gives zero drive torque when the pendulum hangs vertically.

commonErrors.description: Makes the bob lean in the direction of support acceleration.
commonErrors.consequence: The fictitious-force direction is reversed.

problems.flawedProof: Horizontal support acceleration contributes $-\ddot X\sin\theta$, so it cannot perturb a vertical pendulum and the equilibrium leans right.

problems.title: A spherical holonomic constraint, its multiplier force, and the contact model it cannot hide
problems.objective: Derive constrained Euler--Lagrange motion for a particle on a sphere from an augmented action, solve the multiplier from the differentiated constraint, interpret its sign and dimensions as a bilateral reaction, and identify when the same state is impossible for a unilateral string or contact model.
problems.statement:
A particle of mass $m$ moves in a uniform gravitational field near Earth's
surface. Use an inertial Cartesian frame with upward unit vector
$\hat{\mathbf z}$, position $\mathbf r=(x,y,z)$, and potential
$V=mgz$. The particle is trapped by an ideal, fixed, frictionless,
bilateral spherical guide of radius $a$ centered at the origin:
$$
f(\mathbf r)=\mathbf r\cdot\mathbf r-a^2=0.
$$
The guide may push or pull normally; this assumption is deliberate.

Starting from an augmented action with
$$
L_\lambda=\frac12m\dot{\mathbf r}^{2}-mgz
+\lambda(t)(\mathbf r^2-a^2),
$$
perform the independent variations in $\mathbf r$ and $\lambda$. Derive the
equation of motion and both velocity- and acceleration-level constraint
relations. Eliminate the unknown radial acceleration to obtain $\lambda$ in
terms of $z$ and $v=|\dot{\mathbf r}|$. Identify the physical constraint force,
its direction, and the SI dimensions of $\lambda$.

Prove that the constraint force does no instantaneous work on an admissible
trajectory and that the mechanical energy is conserved. Explain why setting
$\delta\mathbf r$ tangent to the sphere from the beginning loses the normal
force but still gives the same tangential dynamics.

At an instant when
$$
z=\frac a2,
\qquad
v^2=\frac{ga}{4},
$$
compute $\lambda$ and the magnitude and direction of the guide force. Then use
$m=2.00\ \mathrm{kg}$, $a=0.800\ \mathrm m$, and
$g=9.81\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$ for numerical values.

Finally replace the bilateral guide by a massless taut string of length $a$
attached to the origin. The string can pull inward but cannot push outward.
Decide whether the same instantaneous state can satisfy that model. State the
correct consequence if the required multiplier has the forbidden sign rather
than silently continuing the constrained equations.
permittedResults: Variation of $L+\lambda f(q)$ gives $dL_{\dot q}/dt-L_q=\lambda\nabla f$ in the sign convention used here, together with $f(q)=0$.
Differentiating $\mathbf r^2=a^2$ twice gives $\mathbf r\cdot\dot{\mathbf r}=0$ and $\mathbf r\cdot\ddot{\mathbf r}=-\dot{\mathbf r}^{2}$.
problems.strategy: Use Cartesian multiplier variation exactly as posed, then differentiate the spherical constraint to eliminate radial acceleration. Project Newton's law into tangent and normal components, provided the augmented-action derivation, multiplier normalization, energy proof, and unilateral boundary are also supplied.
hints: The gradient of the chosen constraint is $2\mathbf r$, so keep the factor of two when identifying the physical reaction.
Dot the vector equation of motion with $\mathbf r$ and use the second derivative of the constraint to solve for $\lambda$.
A string tension has force $-T\mathbf r/a$ with $T\ge0$. Compare that allowed direction with the sign of $2\lambda\mathbf r$ at the specified state.
problems.solution:
Varying the augmented action with endpoint-fixed
$\delta\mathbf r$ gives
$$
\delta S=\int\left[-m\ddot{\mathbf r}-mg\hat{\mathbf z}
+2\lambda\mathbf r\right]\cdot\delta\mathbf r\,dt
+\int(\mathbf r^2-a^2)\,\delta\lambda\,dt.
$$
Independent variations therefore imply
$$
\boxed{m\ddot{\mathbf r}=-mg\hat{\mathbf z}+2\lambda\mathbf r},
\qquad
\boxed{\mathbf r^2=a^2}.
$$
With this normalization of $f$, the physical guide reaction is
$$
\mathbf R=2\lambda\mathbf r.
$$

Differentiating the constraint once and twice yields
$$
\mathbf r\cdot\dot{\mathbf r}=0,
\qquad
\dot{\mathbf r}^{2}+\mathbf r\cdot\ddot{\mathbf r}=0.
$$
Thus $\mathbf r\cdot\ddot{\mathbf r}=-v^2$. Dotting the equation of motion
with $\mathbf r$ gives
$$
-mv^2=-mgz+2\lambda a^2,
$$
and hence
$$
\boxed{\lambda=\frac{m(gz-v^2)}{2a^2}},
\qquad
\boxed{\mathbf R=\frac{m(gz-v^2)}{a^2}\mathbf r}.
$$
Positive $\lambda$ is outward in this convention and negative $\lambda$ is
inward. Since $\lambda f$ has energy dimensions and $f$ has dimensions
$\mathrm m^2$, $[\lambda]=\mathrm{J/m^2}=\mathrm{N/m}$; multiplying by
$2\mathbf r$ gives force.

The instantaneous constraint power is
$$
\mathbf R\cdot\dot{\mathbf r}
=2\lambda\mathbf r\cdot\dot{\mathbf r}=0.
$$
Therefore
$$
\frac d{dt}\left(\frac12mv^2+mgz\right)
=\dot{\mathbf r}\cdot(m\ddot{\mathbf r}+mg\hat{\mathbf z})
=\dot{\mathbf r}\cdot\mathbf R=0.
$$
If variations are restricted to the tangent plane, then
$\mathbf r\cdot\delta\mathbf r=0$ and the normal reaction disappears from
the virtual-work equation. The remaining projected equation determines the
same tangential acceleration, but it cannot determine the force needed to
enforce the embedding constraint; the multiplier method retains that
information.

At the specified state,
$$
gz-v^2=\frac{ga}{2}-\frac{ga}{4}=\frac{ga}{4},
$$
so
$$
\boxed{\lambda=\frac{mg}{8a}},
\qquad
\boxed{\mathbf R=\frac{mg}{4a}\mathbf r},
\qquad
\boxed{|\mathbf R|=\frac{mg}{4}}.
$$
The reaction points radially outward. Numerically,
$$
\lambda=\frac{(2.00)(9.81)}{8(0.800)}
=\boxed{3.065625\ \mathrm{N/m}},
\qquad
|\mathbf R|=\frac{(2.00)(9.81)}4
=\boxed{4.905\ \mathrm N}.
$$

A taut string supplies
$$
\mathbf R_{\rm string}=-T\frac{\mathbf r}{a},\qquad T\ge0,
$$
which is inward only. The state above requires an outward force and therefore
would correspond to $T<0$, impossible for a string. The equality-constrained
string model must stop at the loss-of-tension boundary: the string goes slack
and the particle thereafter follows unconstrained ballistic motion until a
later geometric event. One may not preserve $\mathbf r^2=a^2$ by allowing an
unphysical compressive string.
rubricCriteria: Varies the augmented action independently in $\mathbf r$ and $\lambda$, retaining the reaction $2\lambda\mathbf r$.
Differentiates the spherical constraint twice and obtains $\lambda=m(gz-v^2)/(2a^2)$ with zero guide power.
Computes $\lambda=3.065625\,\mathrm{N/m}$ and $|\mathbf R|=4.905\,\mathrm N$ outward, then enforces string slackness.

commonErrors.description: Drops the factor $2$ from $\nabla(\mathbf r^2-a^2)$ or reverses the reaction sign relative to the stated augmented action.
commonErrors.consequence: The guide force normalization and its outward numerical direction are both wrong.

commonErrors.description: Interprets the required outward guide reaction as an admissible positive string tension.
commonErrors.consequence: The unilateral string is allowed to push, so the necessary slack-detachment transition is missed.

problems.flawedProof: The augmented term gives force $\lambda\mathbf r$, so at the stated state the reaction is inward and a taut string can maintain the motion with positive tension.

problems.title: A nonintegrable velocity constraint conserves energy without defining a surface
problems.objective: Nonintegrable velocity constraints require d'Alembert reactions that do no work without defining a configuration surface.
problems.statement: A particle of mass $m$ has free kinetic Lagrangian $m(\dot x^2+\dot y^2+\dot z^2)/2$ and nonholonomic constraint $\dot y-(x/\ell_0)\dot z=0$, where $\ell_0$ is a fixed length. Apply Lagrange-d'Alembert to derive the multiplier and accelerations. Show the reaction does zero power and that the constraint is not the derivative of $y-(x/\ell_0)z=\text{constant}$. At a state with $m=1.00\,\mathrm{kg}$, $\ell_0=1.00\,\mathrm m$, $x=1.00\,\mathrm m$, $\dot x=2.00\,\mathrm{m/s}$, and $\dot z=3.00\,\mathrm{m/s}$, compute the required $\dot y$, multiplier, and acceleration.
permittedResults: The multiplier force is proportional to the constraint covector $(0,1,-x/\ell_0)$.
Differentiate the velocity constraint along a valid motion.
problems.strategy: First: Write the three multiplier equations and differentiate the velocity constraint. Next: Solve the resulting scalar equation for the multiplier. Finally: Dot reaction with velocity and compare the actual constraint with the derivative of the tempting positional expression.
hints: Write the three multiplier equations and differentiate the velocity constraint.
Solve the resulting scalar equation for the multiplier.
Dot reaction with velocity and compare the actual constraint with the derivative of the tempting positional expression.
problems.solution:
Lagrange-d'Alembert gives $m\ddot x=0$, $m\ddot y=\lambda$, and $m\ddot z=-\lambda x/\ell_0$. Differentiating $\dot y-(x/\ell_0)\dot z=0$ gives $\ddot y-(\dot x/\ell_0)\dot z-(x/\ell_0)\ddot z=0$, hence
$\boxed{\lambda=\dfrac{m\dot x\dot z/\ell_0}{1+x^2/\ell_0^2}}$.
At the stated state, $\dot y=(x/\ell_0)\dot z=\boxed{3.00\,\mathrm{m/s}}$, $\lambda=6/2=\boxed{3.00\,\mathrm N}$, and
$(\ddot x,\ddot y,\ddot z)=\boxed{(0,3.00,-3.00)\,\mathrm{m/s^2}}$. Reaction power is $\lambda[\dot y-(x/\ell_0)\dot z]=0$, so kinetic energy is conserved. But $d[y-(x/\ell_0)z]/dt=\dot y-(x/\ell_0)\dot z-(\dot x/\ell_0)z$, which is not generally zero; the velocity constraint does not define that positional surface.
rubricCriteria: Writes the three multiplier equations and differentiate the velocity constraint.
Solves the resulting scalar equation for the multiplier.
Dots reaction with velocity and compare the actual constraint with the derivative of the tempting positional expression.

commonErrors.description: Integrates the velocity constraint as if the coefficient $x$ were constant.
commonErrors.consequence: It imposes an extra position restriction and changes the dynamics.

commonErrors.description: Claims nonzero multiplier force must change kinetic energy.
commonErrors.consequence: It overlooks zero virtual power along admissible velocities.

problems.flawedProof: The constraint integrates to $y-(x/\ell_0)z=C$, so ordinary holonomic elimination applies. The multiplier is $m\dot x\dot z/\ell_0$ and necessarily dissipates energy.

problems.title: The constrained second variation gives the true stability curvature
problems.objective: Tangent-space second variation gives the true constrained stability threshold and small-oscillation frequency.
problems.statement: A particle of mass $m$ is constrained to a circle $x=R\sin\theta$, $y=-R\cos\theta$ and has potential $U=mgy+\kappa x^2/2$, where $\kappa$ may be negative. Derive the exact reduced potential and the small-oscillation stability criterion at the bottom. For $m=1.00\,\mathrm{kg}$, $R=1.00\,\mathrm m$, and $\kappa=-5.00\,\mathrm{N/m}$, compute the small-oscillation frequency. Explain why inspecting the unconstrained Cartesian Hessian alone can give the wrong answer.
permittedResults: Stability of a one-coordinate equilibrium requires positive reduced-potential curvature.
The kinetic coefficient is $mR^2$.
problems.strategy: First: Substitute the circle exactly into the potential before differentiating. Next: Evaluate the second derivative at the bottom and divide by the generalized inertia. Finally: Compare constrained tangent curvature with arbitrary Cartesian variations that violate the circle.
hints: Substitute the circle exactly into the potential before differentiating.
Evaluate the second derivative at the bottom and divide by the generalized inertia.
Compare constrained tangent curvature with arbitrary Cartesian variations that violate the circle.
problems.solution:
The reduced potential is
$U(\theta)=-mgR\cos\theta+\tfrac12\kappa R^2\sin^2\theta$.
At $\theta=0$, $U'(0)=0$ and
$U''(0)=mgR+\kappa R^2$. Stability requires
$\boxed{mgR+\kappa R^2>0}$, and the small-oscillation frequency is
$\omega^2=U''(0)/(mR^2)=g/R+\kappa/m$.
For the data, $\omega^2=9.81-5.00=4.81\,\mathrm{s^{-2}}$, so $\boxed{\omega=2.193\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}}$. The Cartesian Hessian tests displacements normal as well as tangent to the circle; normal variations are forbidden and their curvature is irrelevant. At the threshold $\kappa=-mg/R$, the quadratic restoring term vanishes and higher-order terms decide behavior.
rubricCriteria: Substitutes the circle exactly into the potential before differentiating.
Evaluates the second derivative at the bottom and divide by the generalized inertia.
Compares constrained tangent curvature with arbitrary Cartesian variations that violate the circle.

commonErrors.description: Uses only gravitational curvature and ignores the constrained quadratic potential.
commonErrors.consequence: Constraint-dependent curvature is lost, so the stiffness threshold is absent.

commonErrors.description: Tests arbitrary Cartesian directions instead of tangent variations.
commonErrors.consequence: It includes physically inadmissible perturbations in the stability verdict.

problems.flawedProof: The Cartesian potential is unbounded when $\kappa<0$, so the bottom is always unstable. Constraints cannot change a Hessian stability classification.

problems.title: Maupertuis refraction bends a trajectory across a potential step
problems.objective: Maupertuis stationarity preserves tangential momentum across a potential step and predicts refraction or reflection.
problems.statement: At fixed total energy $E$, a particle crosses a straight interface between two regions of constant potentials $U_1$ and $U_2<E$. Using the abbreviated action $\int\sqrt{2m(E-U)}\,ds$, derive the mechanical refraction law relating incidence and transmission angles measured from the interface normal. For $E=10.0\,\mathrm J$, $U_1=2.00\,\mathrm J$, $U_2=6.00\,\mathrm J$, and $\theta_1=30.0^\circ$, find $\theta_2$. Interpret bending direction and the threshold for no transmitted classical path.
permittedResults: Stationarity of a broken straight path at a movable interface point conserves tangential canonical momentum.
Momentum magnitude is $p=\sqrt{2m(E-U)}$.
problems.strategy: First: Vary the crossing point along the interface while keeping endpoints fixed. Next: Equate tangential momentum components on the two sides. Finally: Cancel the common mass factor, evaluate the sine relation, and inspect when its right side exceeds one.
hints: Vary the crossing point along the interface while keeping endpoints fixed.
Equate tangential momentum components on the two sides.
Cancel the common mass factor, evaluate the sine relation, and inspect when its right side exceeds one.
problems.solution:
Variation of the crossing point gives continuity of tangential momentum:
$\boxed{p_1\sin\theta_1=p_2\sin\theta_2}$, where $p_i=\sqrt{2m(E-U_i)}$. Thus
$\sin\theta_2=\sqrt{(E-U_1)/(E-U_2)}\sin\theta_1=\sqrt{8/4}(1/2)=1/\sqrt2$,
so $\boxed{\theta_2=45.0^\circ}$. Momentum and speed are lower in the higher-potential region, so the path bends away from the normal. If the computed sine exceeds one, no real transmitted extremal exists for that incidence; the classical path reflects at the step. If $U_1=U_2$, the angle is unchanged.
rubricCriteria: Varies the crossing point along the interface while keeping endpoints fixed.
Equates tangential momentum components on the two sides.
Cancels the common mass factor, evaluate the sine relation, and inspect when its right side exceeds one.

commonErrors.description: Equates normal rather than tangential momentum across the interface.
commonErrors.consequence: It obtains the reciprocal refraction law and wrong bending direction.

commonErrors.description: Uses potential itself instead of kinetic energy difference in momentum magnitude.
commonErrors.consequence: The law fails the equal-potential and accessibility limits.

problems.flawedProof: Normal momentum is conserved, so $p_1\cos\theta_1=p_2\cos\theta_2$. This gives bending toward the normal in the higher-potential region.

problems.title: Two coupled rod constraints require two interacting multipliers
problems.objective: Cartesian multiplier variation for a double pendulum derives coupled constraint reactions, acceleration-level conditions, zero reaction power, and bottom-state tensions.
problems.statement:
A planar double pendulum consists of masses $m_1,m_2$ at Cartesian positions $\mathbf r_1,\mathbf r_2$ in an inertial frame with upward unit vector $\hat{\mathbf y}$. Massless rigid rods have lengths $\ell_1,\ell_2$ and impose
$$
f_1=\mathbf r_1^2-\ell_1^2=0,
\qquad
f_2=(\mathbf r_2-\mathbf r_1)^2-\ell_2^2=0.
$$
Use the augmented Lagrangian
$$
L_*=\frac12m_1\dot{\mathbf r}_1^2+\frac12m_2\dot{\mathbf r}_2^2
-m_1g y_1-m_2g y_2+\frac12\lambda_1f_1+\frac12\lambda_2f_2.
$$
Vary all coordinates and multipliers independently. Derive both vector equations, the velocity- and acceleration-level constraints, and the linear system that determines $\lambda_1,\lambda_2$ from an admissible instantaneous state. Prove that total constraint power is zero.

At the bottom configuration
$$
\mathbf r_1=(0,-\ell_1),
\qquad
\mathbf r_2-\mathbf r_1=(0,-\ell_2),
$$
with both velocities zero, take $m_1=m_2=1.00\,\mathrm{kg}$, $\ell_1=\ell_2=1.00\,\mathrm m$, and $g=9.81\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$. Compute both multipliers, physical rod tensions, and accelerations. Explain the multiplier dimensions and sign convention.
permittedResults: Twice differentiating $\mathbf d^2=\ell^2$ gives $\mathbf d\cdot\ddot{\mathbf d}=-|\dot{\mathbf d}|^2$.
problems.strategy: Keep the two constraint gradients separate in each particle equation. Differentiate both geometric equalities to acceleration level, substitute the vector dynamics, and interpret multiplier signs only after reconstructing the physical rod forces.
hints: Let $\mathbf d=\mathbf r_2-\mathbf r_1$; variation gives forces $-\lambda_2\mathbf d$ on mass 1 and $+\lambda_2\mathbf d$ on mass 2.
The constraints imply $\mathbf r_1\cdot\ddot{\mathbf r}_1=-|\dot{\mathbf r}_1|^2$ and $\mathbf d\cdot(\ddot{\mathbf r}_2-\ddot{\mathbf r}_1)=-|\dot{\mathbf d}|^2$.
At the stationary bottom state, the lower rod supports only mass 2 while the upper rod supports both masses.
problems.solution:
Independent variation gives the constraints and
$$
\boxed{m_1\ddot{\mathbf r}_1=-m_1g\hat{\mathbf y}
+\lambda_1\mathbf r_1-\lambda_2\mathbf d},
$$
$$
\boxed{m_2\ddot{\mathbf r}_2=-m_2g\hat{\mathbf y}
+\lambda_2\mathbf d},
\qquad
\mathbf d=\mathbf r_2-\mathbf r_1.
$$
The first derivatives are
$$
\mathbf r_1\cdot\dot{\mathbf r}_1=0,
\qquad
\mathbf d\cdot\dot{\mathbf d}=0,
$$
and the acceleration constraints are
$$
\boxed{\mathbf r_1\cdot\ddot{\mathbf r}_1=-|\dot{\mathbf r}_1|^2},
\qquad
\boxed{\mathbf d\cdot(\ddot{\mathbf r}_2-\ddot{\mathbf r}_1)=-|\dot{\mathbf d}|^2}.
$$
Substituting the two vector equations into these scalar relations produces a $2\times2$ linear system for $\lambda_1,\lambda_2$ at any regular admissible state; its coefficients are the mass-weighted dot products of the two constraint gradients. This construction retains their coupling automatically.
Explicitly,
$$
\boxed{
\begin{pmatrix}
\ell_1^2&-\mathbf r_1\cdot\mathbf d\\
-(\mathbf r_1\cdot\mathbf d)/m_1&
\ell_2^2(1/m_1+1/m_2)
\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix}\lambda_1\\\lambda_2\end{pmatrix}
=
\begin{pmatrix}
m_1(g y_1-|\dot{\mathbf r}_1|^2)\\
-|\dot{\mathbf d}|^2
\end{pmatrix}}.
$$

Constraint power is
$$
(\lambda_1\mathbf r_1-\lambda_2\mathbf d)\cdot\dot{\mathbf r}_1
+(\lambda_2\mathbf d)\cdot\dot{\mathbf r}_2
=\lambda_1\mathbf r_1\cdot\dot{\mathbf r}_1
+\lambda_2\mathbf d\cdot\dot{\mathbf d}=0.
$$
Thus ideal rods exchange forces but perform no net instantaneous work.

At the stationary collinear bottom state with unit lengths and masses, the equations are purely vertical. The acceleration constraints require zero acceleration along both rods. Writing downward as negative $y$, they yield
$$
\lambda_1-\lambda_2=-g,
\qquad
\lambda_1=2\lambda_2.
$$
Therefore
$$
\boxed{\lambda_2=-g=-9.81\,\mathrm{N/m}},
\qquad
\boxed{\lambda_1=-2g=-19.62\,\mathrm{N/m}}.
$$
Because each multiplier multiplies a length vector to give force, its units are $\mathrm{N/m}$. Negative $\lambda_i$ in the stated $+\lambda_i f_i/2$ convention gives tensile force. The physical tensions are
$$
