\boxed{T_2=-\lambda_2\ell_2=9.81\,\mathrm N},
\qquad
\boxed{T_1=-\lambda_1\ell_1=19.62\,\mathrm N}.
$$
They balance the lower mass's weight and the combined weight transmitted through the upper rod, so
$\boxed{\ddot{\mathbf r}_1=\ddot{\mathbf r}_2=\mathbf0}$ at that instant.
rubricCriteria: Varies both constraint terms with their correct equal-and-opposite lower-rod forces.
Uses both acceleration constraints to define the coupled multiplier solve and proves zero reaction power.
Computes multiplier signs, units, physical tensions, and bottom-state accelerations consistently.

commonErrors.description: Applies the lower-rod multiplier in the same direction to both masses.
commonErrors.consequence: The internal rod force creates net external momentum and the multiplier system is wrong.

commonErrors.description: Sets both second derivatives of the length vectors perpendicular to the rods without the velocity-squared curvature terms.
commonErrors.consequence: Moving configurations receive incorrect radial accelerations and tensions.

problems.flawedProof: Both rods pull each mass downward because the same multiplier sign appears in both constraints. Also $\mathbf r_1\cdot\ddot{\mathbf r}_1=0$ and $\mathbf d\cdot\ddot{\mathbf d}=0$ for every motion, so the two multipliers can be solved independently.

problems.title: A singular Lagrangian hides an arbitrary gauge function
problems.objective: Singular-Hessian equations reveal an arbitrary-function gauge orbit and the failure of initial-data uniqueness without fixing.
problems.statement: Consider $L=(\dot q_1-q_2)^2/2$. Derive both Euler-Lagrange equations and show that one is the time derivative of the other. Prove invariance under $q_1\mapsto q_1+\epsilon(t)$ and $q_2\mapsto q_2+\dot\epsilon(t)$ for arbitrary smooth $\epsilon$. Characterize all solutions and compute the velocity Hessian rank. Explain why specifying $q_1(0)$ and $\dot q_1(0)$ cannot determine a unique trajectory without gauge fixing.
permittedResults: The velocity Hessian has entries $\partial^2L/\partial\dot q_i\partial\dot q_j$.
A transformation that leaves the combination $\dot q_1-q_2$ unchanged leaves $L$ unchanged.
problems.strategy: First: Vary each coordinate separately, noting that the second has no velocity in the Lagrangian. Next: Check the arbitrary-function transformation on the single combination appearing in $L$. Finally: Solve the algebraic Euler-Lagrange constraint first and count the Hessian rank and free function.
hints: Vary each coordinate separately, noting that the second has no velocity in the Lagrangian.
Check the arbitrary-function transformation on the single combination appearing in $L$.
Solve the algebraic Euler-Lagrange constraint first and count the Hessian rank and free function.
problems.solution:
For $q_1$, Euler-Lagrange gives $d(\dot q_1-q_2)/dt=0$. For $q_2$, it gives the stronger algebraic equation
$\boxed{\dot q_1-q_2=0}$; its derivative is the first equation, so they are dependent. Under the stated transformation,
$\dot q_1+\dot\epsilon-(q_2+\dot\epsilon)=\dot q_1-q_2$, proving gauge invariance. Every smooth function $f(t)$ defines a solution
$\boxed{q_1=f(t),\quad q_2=\dot f(t)}$.
The velocity Hessian is $\operatorname{diag}(1,0)$ and has rank one rather than two. Initial $q_1$ and $\dot q_1$ fix only $f(0)$ and $\dot f(0)$; higher behavior remains arbitrary because different gauge functions share those values. A gauge condition is needed for uniqueness, and it must not be mistaken for a new physical equation.
rubricCriteria: Varies each coordinate separately, noting that the second has no velocity in the Lagrangian.
Checks the arbitrary-function transformation on the single combination appearing in $L$.
Solves the algebraic Euler-Lagrange constraint first and count the Hessian rank and free function.

commonErrors.description: Treats the two Euler-Lagrange equations as independent evolution equations.
commonErrors.consequence: It overdetermines a system whose singular Hessian carries gauge freedom.

commonErrors.description: Allows only constant gauge parameters.
commonErrors.consequence: Arbitrary-function gauge freedom is reduced to constants, producing false uniqueness.

problems.flawedProof: The equations independently imply $\ddot q_1=0$ and $q_2=0$, so the unique solution is uniform $q_1$. The Hessian is the identity and there is no gauge freedom.

problems.title: Jacobi's metric turns fixed-energy trajectories into geodesics
problems.objective: Fixed-energy Maupertuis reduction constructs Jacobi's metric, physical-time recovery, and regular turning-point boundary.
problems.statement: For a natural system $L=m|\dot{\mathbf q}|^2/2-U(\mathbf q)$ at fixed energy $E>U$, eliminate time from Maupertuis' abbreviated action and derive the Jacobi line element. Show how physical time is recovered along a geodesic. Apply the construction to one-dimensional $U(q)=kq^2/2$ with energy $E$, identify the allowed interval and explain why the metric degenerates at turning points even though the physical solution is regular. For $k=8.00\,\mathrm{N/m}$ and $E=16.0\,\mathrm J$, compute the turning positions.
permittedResults: At fixed energy, speed satisfies $m v^2/2=E-U$.
Abbreviated action is $\int\mathbf p\cdot d\mathbf q$.
problems.strategy: First: Replace momentum magnitude using the fixed-energy speed relation. Next: Read the resulting path functional as a Riemannian length up to an irrelevant constant factor. Finally: Recover time from distance divided by speed and inspect the zero-kinetic-energy endpoints.
hints: Replace momentum magnitude using the fixed-energy speed relation.
Read the resulting path functional as a Riemannian length up to an irrelevant constant factor.
Recover time from distance divided by speed and inspect the zero-kinetic-energy endpoints.
problems.solution:
Along a fixed-energy path, $|\mathbf p|=mv=\sqrt{2m(E-U)}$, so
$W=\int\sqrt{2m(E-U)}\,ds$. Its stationary paths are geodesics of the Jacobi metric
$\boxed{d\ell_J^2=2m(E-U)\,d\mathbf q^2}$.
Once the oriented path is known, physical time follows from
$\boxed{dt=\sqrt{m/[2(E-U)]}\,ds}$. For $U=kq^2/2$, allowed motion has $|q|\le\sqrt{2E/k}$. The data give
$q_\pm=\pm\sqrt{32/8}=\boxed{\pm2.00\,\mathrm m}$. At a turning point $E-U=0$, the Jacobi metric vanishes and the time integrand diverges like an integrable inverse square root. The geometric parameterization degenerates there, but the oscillator reverses smoothly with finite acceleration.
rubricCriteria: Replaces momentum magnitude using the fixed-energy speed relation.
Reads the resulting path functional as a Riemannian length up to an irrelevant constant factor.
Recovers time from distance divided by speed and inspect the zero-kinetic-energy endpoints.

commonErrors.description: Uses total energy rather than kinetic energy in the Jacobi conformal factor.
commonErrors.consequence: Forbidden regions and turning points disappear from the geometry.

commonErrors.description: Interprets metric degeneracy as a physical trajectory singularity.
commonErrors.consequence: It confuses a fixed-energy reparameterization boundary with divergent acceleration.

problems.flawedProof: The Jacobi metric is $2mE\,dq^2$, independent of potential. It stays nondegenerate at turning points, where the physical acceleration diverges.

problems.title: Inverse-square homogeneity yields a conserved dilation charge
problems.objective: Inverse-square scaling leaves the action invariant and produces the conserved dilation charge with correct time weight.
problems.statement: Let $L=T-U$ with constant mass matrix and a potential homogeneous of degree $-2$. Show that the combined infinitesimal scaling $\delta\mathbf q=\epsilon\mathbf q$, $\delta t=2\epsilon t$ leaves the action invariant. Derive the corresponding conserved dilation charge and verify it directly from the equations. For a state with $\mathbf q\cdot\mathbf p=18.0\,\mathrm{J\,s}$, energy $E=3.00\,\mathrm J$, and $t=2.00\,\mathrm s$, compute the charge. Explain what changes when the potential degree differs from $-2$.
permittedResults: Under the scaling, velocity has infinitesimal weight $-1$, so kinetic energy has weight $-2$.
Euler homogeneity gives $\mathbf q\cdot\nabla U=-2U$.
problems.strategy: First: Track the scaling of coordinates, time element, velocity, kinetic energy, and potential. Next: Use the Noether charge including the time-transformation term. Finally: Differentiate the candidate charge and apply both Euler's theorem and the energy definition.
hints: Track the scaling of coordinates, time element, velocity, kinetic energy, and potential.
Use the Noether charge including the time-transformation term.
Differentiate the candidate charge and apply both Euler's theorem and the energy definition.
problems.solution:
The finite scaling is $\mathbf q\mapsto\lambda\mathbf q$, $t\mapsto\lambda^2t$. Then velocity scales as $\lambda^{-1}$, so both $T$ and degree-$-2$ $U$ scale as $\lambda^{-2}$, while $dt$ scales as $\lambda^2$; the action is invariant. Noether gives
$\boxed{D=\mathbf q\cdot\mathbf p-2tE}$.
Directly, $d(\mathbf q\cdot\mathbf p)/dt=2T+\mathbf q\cdot\mathbf F=2T-\mathbf q\cdot\nabla U=2T+2U=2E$, hence $\dot D=0$. Numerically, $D=18.0-2(2)(3)=\boxed{6.00\,\mathrm{J\,s}}$. For another homogeneity degree, kinetic and potential terms do not scale with the same action weight under this transformation, leaving a virial-type evolution law rather than a conserved dilation charge.
rubricCriteria: Tracks the scaling of coordinates, time element, velocity, kinetic energy, and potential.
Uses the Noether charge including the time-transformation term.
Differentiates the candidate charge and apply both Euler's theorem and the energy definition.

commonErrors.description: Scales time with the same exponent as position.
commonErrors.consequence: Kinetic and inverse-square potential terms acquire different action weights.

commonErrors.description: Omits the energy-times-time term from the Noether charge.
commonErrors.consequence: The remaining position-momentum contraction changes at twice the energy.

problems.flawedProof: Spatial scaling alone is an action symmetry, so $\mathbf q\cdot\mathbf p$ is conserved. The time coordinate and energy do not enter the charge.

problems.title: The Caldirola-Kanai action embeds linear damping in a time-dependent Lagrangian
problems.objective: Caldirola-Kanai variation embeds linear damping while separating canonical quantities from mechanical momentum and energy.
problems.statement: Consider $L=e^{\gamma t}[m\dot q^2/2-kq^2/2]$ with constants $m,k>0$ and $\gamma>0$. Derive the damped oscillator equation, canonical momentum, and mechanical-energy rate. Explain why the canonical Hamiltonian is not the mechanical energy and why explicit time dependence is essential in this representation. For $m=2.00\,\mathrm{kg}$, $k=18.0\,\mathrm{N/m}$, $\gamma=0.500\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$, $q=0.300\,\mathrm m$, $\dot q=-0.400\,\mathrm{m/s}$, and $t=2.00\,\mathrm s$, compute canonical momentum and instantaneous mechanical power loss.
permittedResults: Canonical momentum is $p=L_{\dot q}$.
Mechanical energy is $E_{\rm mech}=m\dot q^2/2+kq^2/2$.
problems.strategy: First: Differentiate the exponentially weighted momentum before subtracting the coordinate derivative. Next: Derive mechanical power by multiplying the physical equation by velocity. Finally: Evaluate canonical and mechanical quantities separately and compare their time weights.
hints: Differentiate the exponentially weighted momentum before subtracting the coordinate derivative.
Derive mechanical power by multiplying the physical equation by velocity.
Evaluate canonical and mechanical quantities separately and compare their time weights.
problems.solution:
Euler-Lagrange gives
$d(e^{\gamma t}m\dot q)/dt+e^{\gamma t}kq=0$, hence
$\boxed{m\ddot q+m\gamma\dot q+kq=0}$. Canonical momentum is $p=e^{\gamma t}m\dot q$, not mechanical momentum $m\dot q$. Mechanical power is
$\dot E_{\rm mech}=\dot q(m\ddot q+kq)=-m\gamma\dot q^2\le0$.
Numerically, $p=e^1(2)(-0.4)=\boxed{-2.175\,\mathrm{kg\,m/s}}$, while
$\dot E_{\rm mech}=-2(0.5)(0.4)^2=\boxed{-0.160\,\mathrm W}$. The canonical Hamiltonian is $e^{-\gamma t}p^2/(2m)+e^{\gamma t}kq^2/2=e^{\gamma t}E_{\rm mech}$ and is explicitly time dependent. Without that time dependence, a regular one-coordinate natural Lagrangian would conserve its energy and could not reproduce ordinary damping in this form.
rubricCriteria: Differentiates the exponentially weighted momentum before subtracting the coordinate derivative.
Derives mechanical power by multiplying the physical equation by velocity.
Evaluates canonical and mechanical quantities separately and compare their time weights.

commonErrors.description: Cancels the exponential factor before differentiating canonical momentum.
commonErrors.consequence: The damping term disappears from Euler-Lagrange.

commonErrors.description: Identifies canonical momentum and Hamiltonian with their mechanical counterparts.
commonErrors.consequence: Exponential canonical weights disappear and mechanical energy is falsely conserved.

problems.title: A rolling sphere conserves energy on a nonintegrable constraint distribution
problems.objective: Coordinate-free rolling constraints connect translation and rotation, prove ideal zero-power dynamics, and expose nonintegrability through Lie brackets.
problems.statement:
A homogeneous sphere of mass $m$, radius $R$, and isotropic center inertia $I=2mR^2/5$ rolls without slipping on a fixed horizontal plane. Let $\mathbf v_C=(\dot x,\dot y,0)$ be center velocity and let $\boldsymbol\omega$ be angular velocity in space components. The contact point relative to the center is $-R\hat{\mathbf z}$.

Derive the no-slip constraints from zero contact velocity. Let the horizontal contact force be $\mathbf F$. Using Newton--Euler equations, prove that in force-free horizontal motion both $\boldsymbol\omega$ and $\mathbf v_C$ are constant and that the ideal contact force does zero power, without setting the force to zero prematurely.

On the configuration manifold $\mathbb R^2\times SO(3)$, let $E_x,E_y,E_z$ denote infinitesimal space-rotation vector fields with $[E_z,E_x]=E_y$. Show that the allowed fields include
$$
A=E_x-R\partial_y,
\qquad
B=E_y+R\partial_x,
\qquad
C=E_z,
$$
and use $[C,A]$ to prove the rank-three rolling distribution is not integrable.

For $m=5.00\,\mathrm{kg}$, $R=0.200\,\mathrm m$, and $\boldsymbol\omega=(3.00,-4.00,2.00)\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$, compute center velocity, speed, translational energy, rotational energy, and total energy.
permittedResults: For an isotropic sphere, angular momentum about its center is $I\boldsymbol\omega$.
problems.strategy: Start from contact-point kinematics, retain the unknown reaction through the Newton--Euler solve, and treat nonintegrability as failure of bracket closure rather than failure to solve a single differential equation.
hints: No slip gives $\mathbf v_C+\boldsymbol\omega\times(-R\hat{\mathbf z})=0$.
Use $m\dot{\mathbf v}_C=\mathbf F$ and $I\dot{\boldsymbol\omega}=(-R\hat{\mathbf z})\times\mathbf F$.
Although $[C,A]=E_y$, the pure field $E_y$ is not in $\operatorname{span}\{A,B,C\}$ because $B$ necessarily carries $R\partial_x$.
problems.solution:
Zero contact velocity gives
$$
\boxed{\mathbf v_C=R\boldsymbol\omega\times\hat{\mathbf z}},
$$
or
$$
\boxed{\dot x=R\omega_y,
\qquad
\dot y=-R\omega_x}.
$$
The contact power is
$$
\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf v_C
+[(-R\hat{\mathbf z})\times\mathbf F]\cdot\boldsymbol\omega
=\mathbf F\cdot[\mathbf v_C+\boldsymbol\omega\times(-R\hat{\mathbf z})]=0.
$$
Thus ideal static friction may be nonzero while doing zero total power.

Differentiate the constraint and use the dynamics:
$$
mR\dot{\boldsymbol\omega}\times\hat{\mathbf z}=\mathbf F,
\qquad
I\dot{\boldsymbol\omega}=(-R\hat{\mathbf z})\times\mathbf F.
$$
Substitution gives
$$
(I+mR^2)\dot{\boldsymbol\omega}_h=0,
\qquad
I\dot\omega_z=0.
$$
Hence $\boxed{\dot{\boldsymbol\omega}=0}$, then
$\boxed{\dot{\mathbf v}_C=0}$ and in this free case $\mathbf F=0$ follows from the solved dynamics rather than from zero power alone.

The rolling distribution is spanned by $A,B,C$. Because
$$
[C,A]=[E_z,E_x]=E_y,
$$
and pure $E_y$ cannot be written as a combination of $A,B,C$ without also introducing the translation $R\partial_x$, the distribution is not closed under Lie brackets. Frobenius integrability therefore fails: rolling velocities do not arise as tangents to a three-dimensional family of configuration submanifolds.

Numerically,
$$
\mathbf v_C=0.200(-4.00,-3.00,0)
=\boxed{(-0.800,-0.600,0)\,\mathrm{m/s}},
$$
so $\boxed{|\mathbf v_C|=1.00\,\mathrm{m/s}}$ and
$$
T_{\rm trans}=\frac12(5.00)(1.00)^2=\boxed{2.50\,\mathrm J}.
$$
The inertia is
$I=(2/5)(5.00)(0.200)^2=0.0800\,\mathrm{kg\,m^2}$, hence
$$
T_{\rm rot}=\frac12(0.0800)(3^2+(-4)^2+2^2)
=\boxed{1.16\,\mathrm J}.
$$
Therefore $\boxed{T=3.66\,\mathrm J}$, constant in the free rolling motion.
rubricCriteria: Derives both no-slip component constraints and the combined zero-power identity for contact reaction.
Solves Newton--Euler equations to obtain constant angular and center velocities without equating zero power to zero force.
Demonstrates bracket nonclosure and computes all requested velocity and energy values.

commonErrors.description: Sets static friction to zero solely because its contact point has zero velocity.
commonErrors.consequence: Zero reaction power is confused with zero reaction force before the dynamics are solved.

commonErrors.description: Treats the two component rolling constraints as derivatives of two global position-orientation equations.
commonErrors.consequence: The nonclosing Lie bracket is ignored and a nonholonomic distribution is falsely declared holonomic.

problems.flawedProof: Because the contact point is instantaneously at rest, $\mathbf F=0$ for every rolling motion. Integrating $\dot x=R\omega_y$ and $\dot y=-R\omega_x$ gives two global holonomic constraints, so the allowed distribution must be integrable.

problems.title: The harmonic-action second variation changes sign at the first conjugate time
problems.objective: Fixed-endpoint second variation locates the first oscillator conjugate time and distinguishes minima from saddles.
problems.statement: For the harmonic oscillator action $S=\int_0^T m(\dot q^2-\omega^2q^2)/2\,dt$ with fixed endpoints, derive the second variation about a classical path. Use the sharp fixed-endpoint inequality to prove that the action is a strict local minimum for $T<\pi/\omega$, has a zero direction at $T=\pi/\omega$, and has a negative direction for larger $T$. For $\omega=2.00\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$, compute the first conjugate time and give the explicit zero mode. Explain why satisfying Euler-Lagrange alone does not determine minimum versus saddle.
permittedResults: For $\eta(0)=\eta(T)=0$, $\int_0^T\dot\eta^2dt\ge(\pi/T)^2\int_0^T\eta^2dt$.
problems.strategy: First: Expand the quadratic action to second order in a fixed-endpoint variation. Next: Apply the sharp inequality to bound the quadratic form by its lowest sine mode. Finally: Evaluate the threshold and test the first sine mode on both sides of it.
hints: Expand the quadratic action to second order in a fixed-endpoint variation.
Apply the sharp inequality to bound the quadratic form by its lowest sine mode.
Evaluate the threshold and test the first sine mode on both sides of it.
problems.solution:
Because the action is quadratic and the first variation vanishes on a classical path,
$\boxed{\delta^2S=m\int_0^T(\dot\eta^2-\omega^2\eta^2)dt}$.
The fixed-endpoint inequality gives
$\delta^2S\ge m[(\pi/T)^2-\omega^2]\int\eta^2dt$. It is strictly positive for $T<\pi/\omega$. At $T=\pi/\omega$, the mode $\eta(t)=\sin(\pi t/T)=\sin(\omega t)$ has zero second variation. For $T>\pi/\omega$, that same lowest sine mode makes the quadratic form negative. With $\omega=2.00\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$, the first conjugate time is
$\boxed{T_c=\pi/2=1.571\,\mathrm s}$ and zero mode is $\boxed{\eta(t)=\sin2t}$ on $[0,\pi/2]$. Euler-Lagrange supplies stationarity; the second variation determines whether the stationary path is locally minimizing or saddle-like.
rubricCriteria: Expands the quadratic action to second order in a fixed-endpoint variation.
Applies the sharp inequality to bound the quadratic form by its lowest sine mode.
Evaluates the threshold and test the first sine mode on both sides of it.

commonErrors.description: Assumes every classical path minimizes action for every duration.
commonErrors.consequence: It ignores negative directions appearing beyond a conjugate point.

commonErrors.description: Uses a constant variation despite fixed endpoints.
commonErrors.consequence: The proposed test direction is inadmissible and gives the wrong threshold.

problems.flawedProof: The second variation is always $m\int(\dot\eta^2+\omega^2\eta^2)dt>0$, so every oscillator trajectory is a minimum for arbitrary time.

problems.title: A translating magnetic ring exposes gauge shifts in reduced mechanics
problems.objective: Moving-constraint reduction and electromagnetic gauge transformation produce the same bead dynamics while shifting canonical momentum and energy representatives by explicit boundary terms.
problems.statement:
A bead of mass $m$ and charge $q$ is constrained to a circular ring of radius $a$ whose center has prescribed inertial position $(X(t),0)$. Use
$$
x=X(t)+a\cos\theta,
\qquad
y=a\sin\theta.
$$
A uniform magnetic field $B\hat{\mathbf z}$ is represented first in symmetric gauge
$$
\mathbf A_S=\frac B2(-y,x),
$$
with zero scalar potential. Derive the reduced one-coordinate Lagrangian, canonical momentum, and exact equation for $\theta$. Interpret separately the support-acceleration term and magnetic term.

Landau gauge $\mathbf A_L=(0,Bx)$ satisfies $\mathbf A_L=\mathbf A_S+\nabla\chi$ with $\chi=Bxy/2$. Reduce this gauge on the moving ring and prove
$$
L_L=L_S+q\frac d{dt}\chi(\theta,t).
$$
Derive the shifts in canonical momentum and reduced energy, emphasizing the partial time derivative at fixed $\theta$.

For $m=2.00\,\mathrm{kg}$, $q=1.00\,\mathrm C$, $B=3.00\,\mathrm T$, $a=0.500\,\mathrm m$, $X=1.00\,\mathrm m$, $\dot X=4.00\,\mathrm{m/s}$, $\ddot X=1.00\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$, $\theta=60.0^\circ$, and $\dot\theta=0.200\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$, compute $\ddot\theta$, $p_\theta^S$, the gauge momentum shift, and $E_L-E_S$. Check $B\to0$ and $\dot X\to0$.
permittedResults: For $L'=L+dG(q,t)/dt$, $p'=p+G_q$ and $E'=E-G_t$.
problems.strategy: Reduce kinetic and vector-potential terms in one gauge, derive the physical equation before changing gauge, then reduce the scalar gauge function itself so all momentum and energy shifts follow from one total derivative.
hints: The bead speed squared is $\dot X^2-2a\dot X\sin\theta\dot\theta+a^2\dot\theta^2$.
In symmetric gauge, $\mathbf A_S\cdot\mathbf v=B[-a\dot X\sin\theta+a^2\dot\theta+aX\cos\theta\dot\theta]/2$.
On the constraint, $\chi=(B/2)(X+a\cos\theta)(a\sin\theta)$.
problems.solution:
The constrained velocity gives
$$
v^2=\dot X^2-2a\dot X\sin\theta\dot\theta+a^2\dot\theta^2.
$$
Also
$$
\mathbf A_S\cdot\mathbf v
=\frac B2[-a\dot X\sin\theta+a^2\dot\theta
+aX\cos\theta\dot\theta].
$$
Thus
$$
\boxed{L_S=\frac m2(\dot X^2-2a\dot X\sin\theta\dot\theta+a^2\dot\theta^2)
+\frac{qB}{2}[-a\dot X\sin\theta+a^2\dot\theta+aX\cos\theta\dot\theta]}.
$$
The canonical momentum is
$$
\boxed{p_\theta^S=m(a^2\dot\theta-a\dot X\sin\theta)
+\frac{qB}{2}(a^2+aX\cos\theta)}.
$$
Euler--Lagrange cancellations leave
$$
\boxed{ma^2\ddot\theta-ma\ddot X\sin\theta
+qBa\dot X\cos\theta=0}.
$$
The middle term is the tangential inertial effect of support acceleration; the last is the tangential Lorentz force generated by translating the charged bead through the field. Tangential bead motion around a stationary ring produces only a normal magnetic force.

Since $\mathbf A_L-\mathbf A_S=\nabla(Bxy/2)$,
$$
\chi(\theta,t)=\frac B2(X+a\cos\theta)(a\sin\theta),
$$
and substitution gives
$\boxed{L_L=L_S+q\,d\chi/dt}$. Therefore
$$
\boxed{p_\theta^L-p_\theta^S=q\chi_\theta},
\qquad
\boxed{E_L-E_S=-q\chi_t},
$$
where $\chi_t=(Ba/2)\dot X\sin\theta$ holds $\theta$ fixed.

Numerically,
$$
\ddot\theta=\frac{\ddot X}{a}\sin\theta
-\frac{qB\dot X}{ma}\cos\theta
=2(0.8660)-3(4.00)(0.500)
=\boxed{-4.268\,\mathrm{s^{-2}}}.
$$
The symmetric-gauge momentum is
$$
p_\theta^S=2[0.25(0.200)-0.5(4.00)(0.8660)]
+\frac32[0.25+0.5(1.00)(0.500)]
=\boxed{-2.614\,\mathrm{kg\,m^2/s}}.
$$
Furthermore,
$$
\chi_\theta=\frac{Ba}{2}[X\cos\theta+a(\cos^2\theta-\sin^2\theta)]
=0.1875\,\mathrm{T\,m^2},
$$
so
$\boxed{p_\theta^L-p_\theta^S=0.1875\,\mathrm{kg\,m^2/s}}$.
Finally,
$$
\boxed{E_L-E_S=-\frac{qBa\dot X\sin\theta}{2}
=-2.598\,\mathrm J}.
$$
When $B\to0$, only moving-support inertial dynamics remain. When $\dot X\to0$ at the instant, the tangential magnetic term and explicit-time gauge-energy shift vanish, while a nonzero $\ddot X$ may still drive the bead.
rubricCriteria: Reduces both kinetic and symmetric-gauge couplings and derives the exact physical angular equation.
Shows the Landau-gauge reduction differs by the reduced total derivative and obtains both canonical shifts.
Computes acceleration, momentum, gauge momentum shift, energy shift, and both diagnostic limits.

commonErrors.description: Drops the prescribed translation from the vector-potential coupling because the ring shape is unchanged.
commonErrors.consequence: The tangential magnetic drive and gauge energy shift both disappear from a physically moving constraint.

commonErrors.description: Calls canonical momentum and reduced energy gauge invariant after adding $q\,d\chi/dt$.
commonErrors.consequence: Boundary-term shifts are ignored even though the physical equation remains unchanged.

problems.flawedProof: Gauge changes leave every canonical expression numerically identical, so $p_\theta^L=p_\theta^S$ and $E_L=E_S$. Because the ring only translates without changing shape, $\dot X$ cannot enter magnetic force or bead dynamics.
